docs.text:
Opinion 
 Polymarket has its sights set on breaking into Europe. Will the continent's regulators roll the dice?
 Lionel Laurent 3 min read 4 Oct 2026, 03:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 European policymakers are unlikely to view this prediction betting service as just another trading platform, as it claims to be, and wisely so. If Polymarket manages to get a foot in the door, it could unleash chaos. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Head to Polymarket’s US website and you will be greeted with crystal-ball trades on everything from the midterm elections to the likelihood of a fully reopened Strait of Hormuz. Try that in France, and you will see something very different: Sober black-on-white text under the words, “Illegal website.” 
 That’s because in France and other European countries, regulators see prediction markets run by Polymarket and its rival Kalshi as unregulated gambling that dodges the safeguards and oversight of licensed platforms. They also fret, justifiably, about the harm to people from losing money on an addictive , easily manipulated 24x7 market. 
 In April, big bets on the temperature in Paris coincided with suspected weather sensor-tampering at the country’s largest airport. By July, France blocked Polymarket’s site and teamed up with other national watchdogs to warn against prediction markets. The US company is contesting the ban. 
 This may sound familiar, given Brazil’s crackdown on these sites and New York’s recent lawsuit accusing Polymarket of illegal gambling. But the firm is betting on a new path to regulatory acceptance in Europe by going around gambling watchdogs and engaging directly with financial supervisors from the Paris-based European Securities Markets Authority (ESMA) and the UK Financial Conduct Authority. 
 The idea is to convince them that this is a derivatives market, not a gambling one, and should be regulated as such rather than banned. This would mirror its US setup, where prediction markets are overseen federally by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—even as American states argue that these are sports-betting sites and should fall under their purview. 
 This is a bold wager. Polymarket has the cash and lobbying heft to get its foot in the door after a $1 billion funding round led by Donald Trump Jr’s venture-capital firm. It may sway some technocrats by pointing to financial-market bets on its platform where the underlying market is regulated, such as currencies or commodities. 
 ESMA already regulates so-called binary options—a derivative that pays out if a yes-or-no outcome is met. And it has floated the idea that some prediction-market contracts fit this category. 
 Neal Kumar, Polymarket’s chief legal officer, says his business wants “a regulated pathway in Europe for this new asset class.” The firm also sent me poll results from a London firm that found 90% of finance professionals reckoned prediction-market data could inform their trading decisions. 
 Still, one hopes regulators will think hard before accepting what looks like the thin end of a fat wedge. Even before Polymarket and Kalshi, binary options have blurred the lines between investing and betting because of their coin-toss, speculative nature. Most folks lose money on them and they are still deemed too risky for retail investors in the European Union (EU). In Britain, they were once labelled gambling products. 
 Opening the door to more of these via Polymarket feels like an unnecessary step into the unknown. ESMA’s approval could be misinterpreted as a green light for the company and its industry, even if it covered only a narrow subset of what’s out there. 
 As for the argument about treating sports predictions as a derivatives market, good luck with winning that debate in Europe. Sports bets, which account for 80% of prediction markets’ onshore activity, don’t fit the financial-supervision mould. Their oversight is also better established in Europe than in the US. 
 As for the racier trades, from wagering on declarations of war or Christ’s second coming, no number of claims of “informational value ” will be fully persuasive. This stuff can create incentives for corrupt, illegal or dangerous actions to rig the outcome, as a recent paper co-authored by Bocconi University’s Luis Enriques explains. 
 But France-style bans are not the last word. It’s hard to get the EU’s 27 members to agree on regulation. Malta has gone it alone on crypto rules to bring in the industry’s money. And in a world where every few years brings a new form of casino finance, it’s worth sketching out workable regulation besides prohibition. Jackson Gutenplan, a Bloomberg Intelligence analyst, says one endpoint for prediction markets could be strictly regulating trades around politics, climate or corporate events. 
 But that’s a long-term challenge that doesn’t address the central issue today: that Polymarket [activity] still looks more like gambling than investing. The problem is both the speculative element and that the deck is stacked against the consumer , a former senior regulatory official tells me. 
 Country bans create their own difficulties and loopholes, but it still looks like the riskier punt would be rushing to give this market a regulatory blessing. Supervisory dice rolls can wait. ©Bloomberg 
 The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist writing about the future of money and the future of Europe.

docs.title: Is your SBI, HDFC Bank, other bank branch closing or shifting? Will IFSC, cheque book details change? Know here
docs.text:
If your bank tells you that the branch where you hold an account is closing, shifting, or merging with another branch, there is generally no need to withdraw your money or open a fresh account.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) requires banks to inform customers in advance about such changes and make arrangements to ensure that banking services continue. If an account is transferred to another branch of the same bank, it can continue as an existing account rather than being treated as a new one, provided the required KYC formalities are already complete.
What happens to your bank account after the branch closes?
A branch shutting down does not mean that your account or deposit will disappear. The bank will generally transfer the account to another branch or banking outlet and inform customers about the new arrangement.
RBI rules require banks to give customers sufficient notice when a branch is being closed, shifted, or merged, allowing them to make arrangements and avoid disruption to their banking services.
If the account is moved to another branch of the same bank, customers should not ordinarily be asked to open a completely new account merely because of the transfer. RBI has clarified that KYC completed at one branch remains valid when an account is transferred within the same bank, subject to applicable requirements.
Will your IFSC, cheque book and other details change?
Customers should check the details of the branch to which their account has been moved. This includes the new branch address, IFSC, cheque book and passbook requirements, as well as any standing instructions linked to the account.It is also important to check payments that depend on the account. Salary credits, pension payments, EMIs and investment-related transactions should be monitored to ensure they continue without any disruption.
Is a bank merger the same as a branch closure?
No. The closure or shifting of an individual branch is different from the merger of one bank with another.
When RBI approves a bank amalgamation, the scheme specifies how the transferring bank's assets, liabilities and branches will be taken over. In earlier approved mergers, branches of the bank being transferred have continued to operate as branches of the acquiring bank from the effective date of the merger.
Customers should therefore check whether the merger has resulted in changes to their account details, internet banking access, debit cards, cheque books or other banking services. Any revised service terms should also be checked.
What should you do if you receive a suspicious message?
A branch closure or bank merger can sometimes be used by fraudsters to send fake messages asking customers to update their account details or share sensitive information.Do not share your password, PIN or OTP merely because you have received a message about a branch closure or bank merger. Verify any such request through the bank's official communication channels before taking action.What happens to your bank locker if the branch closes?Customers with a safe deposit locker need to pay closer attention when their branch is being closed, shifted or merged.RBI's revised locker instructions specifically cover such situations. The bank is required to issue a public notice in two newspapers, including one local vernacular daily, and inform locker customers at least two months in advance.Customers must also be given the option to change or close the locker facility.Can the bank move your locker to another branch?If the locker facility is being relocated, customers should carefully check the bank's communication to find out where the locker will be housed after the change.They should also confirm how access to the new facility will work and whether any updated documents or agreements need to be signed. The existing locker agreement and key should be kept safely until the transition is complete.What should you check when your branch is shutting down?Once a branch closure, shifting or merger is announced, customers should check whether their registered mobile number, email address and postal address are up to date.Those with pending transactions, dormant accounts, lockers or important standing instructions should contact the bank or visit the new branch to ensure that everything has been transferred correctly.For most customers, a branch closure is an administrative change rather than a loss of their banking relationship. The important thing is to confirm where the account and, if applicable, the locker have been moved, and update your records before the old branch stops operating.

docs.title: Govt proposes safety limits for medicinal plant used for treating epilepsy
docs.text:
Explainer 
 Govt proposes safety limits for medicinal plant used for treating epilepsy
 Dhirendra Kumar 5 min read 4 Oct 2026, 01:39 PM IST 
 Summary
 The draft rules set limits for heavy metals, aflatoxins and pesticide residues in Mundulea sericea as India’s traditional-medicine exports expand. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 New Delhi: The government has proposed a set of safety and quality limits for the root bark of Mundulea sericea, a medicinal plant used in traditional treatment for various conditions, including epilepsy.
 A draft proposal, seen by Mint , sets maximum limits for toxic heavy metals, aflatoxins, pesticide residues and microbial contaminants in the plant material. The proposal has been prepared by the Bureau of Indian Standards’ (BIS) Ayurveda Sectional Committee and is currently under consideration, two government officials said.
 The proposed limits include 10 parts per million (ppm) for lead, 1 ppm for mercury, 0.3 ppm for cadmium and 3 ppm for arsenic. It also sets maximum limits of 2 ppm for aflatoxin B1 and 5 ppm for total aflatoxins.
 The move assumes significance as India seeks to expand the global markets for the traditional medicine sector, where consistent quality and safety standards are important to maintain the sector’s credibility and competitiveness.
 India’s AYUSH services economy stood at $36.92 billion in FY25, while AYUSH product exports rose from $869.81 million in FY21 to $1.27 billion in FY25 before easing marginally to $1.25 billion in FY26, according to government data.
 The proposed norms cover the root bark of Mundulea sericea, a plant belonging to the Fabaceae family, that grows up to 10-15 feet and is found in several parts of Karnataka, including Bagalkote, Belagavi, Ballari, Bijapur, Chikkamagaluru, Chitradurga, Hassan, Kolar, Tumakuru and Uttara Kannada.
 The root bark has traditionally been used for conditions such as epilepsy, poisonous bites, wounds, hernia and infertility, as well as bilharziasis (schistosomiasis). These uses are based on traditional practices and should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical efficacy, said the first of the two officials cited above.
 The draft proposal describes the plant as “extra-pharmacopoeial”, meaning it is not currently included in the official pharmacopoeia.
 From contaminants to plant identification 
 “The proposed standards are intended to ensure that the plant material used in Ayurvedic products meets basic quality and safety requirements, rather than being sold as an unregulated raw material in roadside shops,” said the first official. “This can help consumers get products of consistent quality, while ensuring that manufacturers use properly identified and tested plant material.”
 The root bark must be free from foreign matter and meet set limits for ash and extractives, the officials said. The proposed norms also set microbiological requirements, including the absence of Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Salmonella in specified forms of the material, as well as limits for Escherichia coli, total microbial count, yeast and mould.
 The draft proposal further requires testing for a range of pesticide residues. If pesticides not listed in the standard are used before or after harvesting, the material would also have to be tested under the relevant BIS method , with limits calculated using an acceptable daily intake-based formula.
 To identify the plant material, the proposed norms require high-performance thin-layer chromatography (HPTLC) testing, which creates a chemical “fingerprint” of the root bark. The test would look for 14 spots at 254 nanometres and 9 spots at 366 nanometres, which would be compared with a reference standard to confirm the material's identity.
 HPTLC is a laboratory test used to identify plant materials and check their quality.
 The draft also prescribes packaging requirements including the botanical name, producer or packer’s name and address, batch number, net quantity, state and country of production, packing date and storage instructions.
 The proposed norms are based mainly on the Monographs on Anukta Dravya, Volume 2, published by the Institute for Teaching and Research in Ayurveda, Jamnagar.
 “India is a global leader in Ayurveda and traditional medicine, and as the sector expands its presence in international markets, maintaining consistent standards for quality and safety is critical,” said Dr Rakesh Kotwal, medical officer (ayurveda) at sub-district Hospital (SDH) Padder in the Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir.
 “Developing standards for medicinal plants that are increasingly being used in Ayurvedic formulations can help ensure that consumers get safe and consistent products and strengthen confidence in Indian traditional medicines,” Kotwal said.
 Dr Smita Pankaj Naram, chairperson of ayurvedic healthcare centre chain Ayushakti Ayurveda said, “We follow such testing for all our herbal ingredients, so I support the move to introduce clear standards for medicinal plants. It can help ensure that raw materials are properly tested for contaminants and meet consistent quality requirements before they are used in Ayurvedic products.”
 The Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) estimates that India’s AYUSH services economy stood at $36.92 billion in FY25, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 16.91% since FY23. The study projects the sector to reach $216-318 billion by 2047.
 Queries sent to the department of consumer affairs remained unanswered till the press time.

docs.title: Oil was pouring through the Strait of Hormuz again. Then attacks on shipping resurged.
docs.text:
Global 
 Oil was pouring through the Strait of Hormuz again. Then attacks on shipping resurged.
 Georgi Kantchev , Rebecca Feng , Shelby Holliday , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 5 Oct 2026, 06:43 AM IST 
 Summary
 Iran’s targeting of ships has improved, according to a U.S. official, making transits through the Strait of Hormuz riskier. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—A new wave of attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz is threatening a recovery in Middle Eastern oil exports—just as Gulf producers have pushed crude shipments back toward prewar levels.
 The swift rebound in shipments in recent weeks has been driven by U.S. naval protection helped by earlier waves of strikes that knocked out Iranian radar and communications along the contested strait. The United Arab Emirates and other producers have set up an elaborate system of shuttle runs in which tankers load inside the Persian Gulf, exit Hormuz and transfer the crude to vessels waiting outside the waterway.
 But after several days without reporting attacks on ships toward the end of last month, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations, which is affiliated with the Royal Navy, has reported seven strikes on vessels around the waterway since Sept. 28. On Sunday, it reported another strike, but didn’t say when the incident happened.
 Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy issued a warning to ships planning to use the U.S.-backed route through the strait on Saturday, saying that they would be targeted and destroyed. “Don’t trust U.S. Navy and don’t use south corridor at all and don’t put your life in danger,” a radio message transmitted on a public shipping channel and reviewed by The Wall Street Journal said.
 The renewed attacks may already be taking a toll, with early signs that oil flows are beginning to slow, analysts say. Firm data comes with a lag, because many ships are operating without their transponders switched on to avoid becoming targets.
 All seven vessels were attacked near the narrowest part of the Hormuz strait, according to UKMTO.
 Iran’s ability to target ships has also improved in recent weeks, adding to the risks in the strait, according to a U.S. official. The U.S. several weeks ago said it would strike Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran’s attacks, but it has since backed off that effort after Iran unleashed a wave of missiles at a U.S. air base in Jordan, the official said.
 The new strikes expose the fragility of the recovery in oil flows and come as President Trump, who has claimed full U.S. control over Hormuz, weighs renewed military action against Iran.
 Any fresh disruption would hit a global economy already grappling with high energy and rising borrowing costs. International benchmark oil prices remain around $100 a barrel despite recovering exports, reflecting fears that renewed attacks could again curb flows and keep freight and security costs elevated.
 “The step-up in attacks on ships highlights how the current equilibrium in the oil market is fragile and could easily be shattered,” said Hamad Hussain, a senior economist at Capital Economics. “This would especially be the case if there is further escalation and energy infrastructure is targeted.”
 Brent, the international oil benchmark, settled Friday at $102.25 a barrel, up nearly 5% for the week. Hussain said traders were pricing in a substantial risk that flows would fall again. Capital Economics expects Brent to remain around $100 through the end of the year.
 Among the seven vessels attacked in the past week, at least four had completed two or more roundtrips in and out of Strait of Hormuz since June, carrying crude oil or oil products, according to ship tracker Kpler.
 Al Funtas, a so-called very large crude carrier operated by Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, was completing its fifth shuttle run between the Port of Mina Al-Ahmadi in Kuwait and ports in the Gulf of Oman when it was attacked on Sept. 28, according to Kpler. Kazimah III, another VLCC operated by KOTC, had carried out three shuttle runs and was on its way into the Persian Gulf when it was hit on Oct. 1.
 Ships of that size can carry as many as two million barrels of oil at a time.
 Since the U.S. and Israeli strikes that began the war in February, Iran has used attacks on ships to throttle shipping through Hormuz, once the thoroughfare for a fifth of the world’s oil. That has driven up the price of gasoline and diesel for consumers around the world and has forced Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E. to divert exports around the strait through bypass pipelines.
 Kpler said regional crude exports excluding Iran averaged at least 16.5 million barrels a day from Sept. 1 through Sept. 28, close to prewar levels.
 But there are signs Iran’s recent attacks may already be starting to slow that recovery.
 Rory Johnston, founder of oil research firm Commodity Context, said he has seen a potential pullback in recent days and estimates flows are down by two million to three million barrels a day, though those initial totals could be revised higher as better information becomes available.
 “The recent pace of flows, while impressive, has never been sustainable and has already come at great expense,” Johnston said. Part of the surge may reflect exporters rushing barrels out before a feared new escalation, he said. Gulf oil producers are shelling out between $30 million to $40 million for a round trip shuttle run in and out of Hormuz—or $15 to $20 a barrel, according to shipbrokers, and that figure doesn’t include insurance costs.
 Saudi Arabia had shifted exports back through Hormuz after a Sept. 10 attack on its East-West pipeline and attacks on its ships by Yemen’s Houthi militants interrupted Red Sea shipments. The pipeline remains below capacity, but renewed loading at the Yanbu port on the Red Sea could help offset another Hormuz slowdown, Hussain said.

docs.title: Multiple security failures allowed FlyDubai pilot into cockpit
docs.text:
Global 
 Multiple security failures allowed FlyDubai pilot into cockpit
 Summer Said , Anat Peled , Benoit Faucon , The Wall Street Journal 8 min read 5 Oct 2026, 06:53 AM IST 
 Summary
 Authorities in three countries missed opportunities across the board; “there wasn’t proper vetting.” 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—Before Hamam al-Hammami stood behind his captain on FlyDubai Flight 1073 and raised an emergency ax to begin the assault that nearly brought down the plane, there had been ample opportunity for authorities in three countries to keep him from getting anywhere near that cockpit.
 Oman had scrutinized his online habits and decided he showed too much interest in radical ideology to trust as a pilot at state carrier Oman Air, where he worked. They banned him from flying, sent him to a deradicalization program and put him in a desk job but didn’t flag their concerns more broadly, people familiar with the matter said.
 When FlyDubai hired him in February, it didn’t contact Oman to vet his experience. The company did do a criminal-background check, a person familiar with the process said. The airline later put him on the sensitive route to Tel Aviv, where he flew multiple times, people familiar with the matter said.
 Emirati authorities are currently investigating FlyDubai staff who were involved in the hiring process, people familiar with the investigation said. FlyDubai said it wouldn’t comment while the investigation was ongoing.
 The last chance to stop him before the airport came in Israel. It was a low bar—pilots from countries like Oman that don’t have diplomatic relations are barred from flying to the country, so Hammami should have been stopped outright.
 Israel requires foreign carriers to submit lists of inbound passengers and crew in advance. FlyDubai sent the manifest for Flight 1073, said Israel’s Tax Authority, which maintains the country’s database of flier information. But the Ministry of Transportation, which oversees foreign carriers, said it didn’t believe it had the authority or required expertise to vet flight crews.
 The ministry has never asked for a passenger or crew list since the database was set up in 2023. It says it didn’t know it could. Instead, the ministry says FlyDubai agreed in writing to check its pilots’ backgrounds and nationalities.
 A classified 2024 report flagged the ministry for failing to adequately secure foreign carriers’ flights.
 With the string of missed opportunities, the dramatic fight for survival by the wounded captain and a handful of passengers is now being overshadowed by a growing realization there was a massive security failure on several fronts.
 Security experts said the failure is remarkable given the surveillance and intelligence capabilities of the U.A.E. and Israel, and the obvious threats to the route the co-pilot was allowed to fly.
 It also points to a conundrum of aviation security. Regulators buffeted by major failures like the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the U.S. and the intentional crash by the co-pilot of Germanwings Flight 9525 in 2015 are caught in a tug of war—protecting against dangerous passengers by securing the cockpit or guarding against rogue pilots by making it easier to intervene.
 Security experts say the onus has to be on intelligence services to identify and stop threats before they ever get to the airport.
 “If this was a dedicated jihadist terror attack, there are multiple levels of failure that happened from an intelligence perspective way before we get to the fact that someone may have missed something in security screening,” said Matthew Borie, chief intelligence officer and co-founder of Osprey Flight Solutions.
 Officials in the U.A.E., Oman and Israel all privately said there were significant failures across the board—from the U.A.E. and Israel’s vetting to Oman’s communication of its concerns about Hammami.
 The U.A.E. declined to comment while the investigation into the incident and its causes is ongoing. A spokeswoman for the Omani government didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday said he ordered a review of the security of foreign airline flights to the country.
 The security missteps culminated in a dramatic series of events a little over halfway into Flight 1073’s trip to Tel Aviv last week. The airplane’s captain, Smit Machchhar, said his co-pilot excused himself to pray then struck him several times with an onboard emergency ax. The pilot managed to open the cockpit door, letting in a group of rescuers who subdued the co-pilot and pulled the plane out of a dangerous dive.
 The U.A.E.’s attorney general said Saturday that the co-pilot had tried to commit an act of terrorism. Saudi Arabia, the U.A.E. and Israel all suspect he was trying to crash the plane in Tel Aviv, people familiar with their thinking said.
 All three are investigating whether he acted alone. They haven’t turned up any links to any foreign power or major terrorist organization, they said.
 Hammami is 29 years old, born to an Omani father and Syrian mother, The Wall Street Journal previously reported.

docs.title: Searching for a lost classic of Bangladeshi cinema
docs.text:
Lounge 
 Searching for a lost classic of Bangladeshi cinema
 Zico Ghosh 7 min read 4 Oct 2026, 12:01 PM IST 
 Summary
 Naeem Mohaiemen’s ‘A Missing Can of Film’ searches the surviving images of director Zahir Raihan, from a lost chapter of Bangladesh’s cinema 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Forty-five days after Bangladesh became independent in December 1971, Zahir Raihan, one of the key figures of Bengali cinema from the region, went missing at the age of 36. He had gone looking for his brother, a writer, who had disappeared during the war. Raihan is suspected to have been abducted and killed, presumably by the Pakistan army.
 That’s the narrative that visual artist and writer Naeem Mohaiemen, 57, says he grew up hearing—even though that did not make sense: how could the Pakistan army operate in a newly independent Bangladesh, let alone murder a prominent figure like Raihan? It’s only in the last 15 years or so that Mohaiemen, who’s based in New York and Dhaka, started to learn about a missing can of film. A film Raihan had made that apparently held secrets that could “embarrass the war command” of the newly formed state. It got Mohaiemen, whose practice has been described as an investigation of “failed leftist utopias and incomplete decolonisations”, interested.
 Raihan’s political commitments were deeper than his filmography might suggest—he made about a dozen films and wrote eight novels. He had been a member of the Communist Party for years, even as he built a successful career making popular cinema: family dramas and entertainers, including Pakistan’s first colour film, Sangam (1964), in Urdu. It was only towards the end of his life that the politics became impossible to separate from the filmmaking.
 Jibon Theke Neya (1970), a domestic melodrama that doubled as an allegory of East Pakistan, marked the turn. During the Liberation War, Raihan moved to Kolkata and became part of the cultural front of the independence movement, making the 20-minute documentary, Stop Genocide , his masterpiece and a landmark political film of the war. He was also involved in several other films during this period, including the unfinished Let There Be Light , which was described as an “ode to human suffering through the ages”, and the film whose supposed existence gives Mohaiemen’s project, its title.
 It is this brief, volatile phase that Mohaiemen is after in his video installation A Missing Can of Film (2025). “I wanted to trace the genealogy of Raihan’s brief, liminal socialist cinema,” he wrote in an essay in February this year for The Daily Star , “or what I call the ‘Socialist Stillborn’ formed under the crucible of a liberation war in which the communist parties were not allowed a central role.” A Missing Can of Film reflects on this unfinished history and the idea of revolution, while attempting to enter his unrealised cinema through the films he left behind. The film is part of Mohaiemen’s exhibition Raihan-Ghatak-Tarkovsky , on at Experimenter, Kolkata, until 10 October.
 Mohaiemen traces that unrealised cinema largely through Raihan’s own images. Archival footage from across his filmography is cut together in unexpected combinations: a scene from one of his Urdu films converses with one from a Bengali film; songs, dances, faces and bodies recur across different films and different registers. There are split-screens, with images playing simultaneously; sometimes one panel goes black while the others continue.
 It becomes a sensory trip through an archive, with Mohaiemen making Raihan’s films speak to one another rather than simply illustrating his story. “In Missing Can I search for Zahir Raihan within his own film archive,” he writes. The language of the film is fluid: archival footage, contemporary images, scraps of sound and text that sometimes resembles inter-titles are spliced together into a shifting tapestry. Visual and aural echoes travel between Raihan’s films and the images Mohaiemen has shot himself.
 Those contemporary images come from the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation (BFDC), filmed in the immediate aftermath of the 2024 student uprising. Rusting equipment, empty spaces, machines and corridors acquire an eerie quality. Mohaiemen lingers over them, allowing the BFDC to become a site from where one political moment contemplates another. In red letters, the film asks: Is this the nation they wanted?
 This encounter between past and present also extends to the way Mohaiemen draws on Raihan’s own cinematic language. A Missing Can of Film begins with a girl working a dheki, the traditional wooden rice-pounding device, its rhythmic thudding establishing the film’s opening soundscape. It recalls Stop Genocide , whose most striking device is the punctuation-like use of “STOP” as in the telegram. In Raihan’s film, the word lands like a command, almost a call to action, interrupting the flow of images and freezing them in place; at the same time, it becomes a literal demand to stop the atrocities being shown.
 Stop Genocide is also striking in the way Raihan frames people. Faces come right up to the lens, often pushed to the edge of the frame, while tents, camps and other figures remain visible behind them. There is something starkly Soviet in these compositions. Bangladeshi film critic and author Mahmudul Hossain, in The Other National Cinema of Bangladesh (2023), argues that Raihan drew on Third Cinema’s use of documentary footage, newsreels, photographs and statistics.
 There is a playfulness to the film even amid the horror, making Stop Genocide an exciting piece of agitprop cinema. Mohaiemen picks up that impulse, allowing images to halt, collide and fracture. He even credits Raihan for screenplay and direction and the original cinematographers for their work, treating the footage as authored material, with its own rhythms, choices and visual logic.

 Lula is the Brazilian Left’s last hope—and its biggest problem
 Samantha Pearson , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 4 Oct 2026, 07:32 AM IST 
 Summary
 The 80-year-old president has crowded out successors. If he loses a re-election bid, it could shut his party out of power for years. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 SÃO PAULO—President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is 80 years old, recovered from brain surgery and convinced that Brazil’s left can’t survive without him.
 The problem for his movement is that he’s probably right.
 A quarter of a century after first winning the presidency, the former union leader is seeking a fourth term, with the first round of voting Sunday set to go to a runoff on Oct. 25. A victory would make da Silva one of the world’s longest-serving democratically elected leaders. He is the last remaining stalwart of South America’s left, which has suffered a string of defeats as the region takes a rightward turn driven by economic and security concerns.
 His enduring grip over Brazil’s left for much of this century now risks the future of the very party he co-founded 46 years ago. Under him, the Workers’ Party has become a central pillar of Brazilian politics, but one with no clear successor and no backup plan if he loses.
 “There are moments in politics, like in soccer, when you don’t have as many star players as you would like,” da Silva told a podcast aired on YouTube recently. For now, he maintains, he is the only person capable of beating the country’s insurgent right wing.
 Sunday’s election—a razor-thin race against Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro—serves as a test of that wager. Da Silva is expected to go through to a runoff with Bolsonaro, but if he loses that race, the country’s left could be shut out of power for years, making it another Latin American political movement that fails to outlive its founders.
 Da Silva’s dominance has proved both the Workers’ Party’s greatest asset and its ultimate weakness. As Brazil’s first working-class president, his personal bond with poorer voters transcends his party’s brand.
 Yet his towering presence has choked off potential heirs. Handpicked successors have either faltered—like Dilma Rousseff, impeached in 2016—or lost, like Fernando Haddad in 2018.
 Brazil’s left turns to da Silva because no one else commands national authority, but each run makes it harder for anyone else to rise up.
 “Lula is perhaps the most important political leader of the century,” said João Paulo Rodrigues, leader of the Landless Workers’ Movement. “Anyone you put next to him looks tiny by comparison.”
 Rodrigues said he would consider running for president one day, but that there was little point in contemplating a post-Lula future before that moment actually arrived. Jokingly citing Karl Marx, he said: “Mankind always sets itself only such tasks as it is able to solve.”
 But with da Silva’s defeat in a likely runoff now a real possibility and new figures fast emerging on the political right, the search for a political heir is more urgent than ever, said Leandro Gabiati, a political scientist and director at Dominium Public Affairs.
 Another term would let da Silva manage the transition from the presidency, but out of power, without the influence and machinery of government, the struggle to find the left’s next torchbearer is set to be far more difficult, Gabiati said.
 With his 10th grandchild on the way, da Silva has gone to great lengths to prove he is still physically fit for the job, brushing aside comparisons with former President Joe Biden and joking that his new wife, 20 years his junior, can vouch for his youthful stamina.
 Concerns about his age resurfaced two years ago following an accident in the palace bathroom—he fell while cutting his nails and underwent emergency surgery to drain a brain bleed. He has since taken to stripping to the waist for social-media videos of himself at the gym pounding a treadmill and doing squats.
 Da Silva is already the longest-serving president in Brazil’s democratic history, surviving a military dictatorship, throat and skin cancers, a vast corruption scandal that landed him in jail in 2018 and an alleged assassination plot by Jair Bolsonaro’s allies. Another four-year term would see him match Angela Merkel’s tenure as chancellor in Germany, surpass every U.S. president, including Franklin D. Roosevelt, and trail only a handful of long-serving leaders in modern democracies—mostly prime ministers who face no constitutional term limits.
 The son of illiterate farmworkers from Brazil’s impoverished northeast, he spent 13 days traveling by truck to São Paulo state as a child before becoming a metalworker, losing a finger in a factory accident and rising through the union movement to the presidency. Even poorer voters who see him as tainted by corruption still view him as the politician most likely to stand up for them in a brutally unequal country, where the poorest half of the population—more than 100 million people—still hold less than 3% of household wealth.
 “The poor always get screwed here but Lula screwed us a bit less,” said Pedro Alves, a construction worker in São Paulo, who said he had managed to put his son into college thanks to a government-backed student loan program expanded under the Workers’ Party.
 Even some of da Silva’s fiercest critics acknowledge him to be a political animal like few others with his instinct for crowds and mastery of Brazil’s transactional politics, turning enemies into allies and holding together unwieldy coalitions.
 That charm has won over a motley crew of foreign leaders. Former President Barack Obama once called him “my man,” Iran’s Mahmoud Ahmadinejad referred to him as a “good friend,” and President Trump declared they had “excellent chemistry” after what he described as just a 39-second enc

 38 years after Ahmedabad crash, Air India seeks fast hearing on compensation formula
 Krishna Yadav 4 min read 5 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 The outcome could shape how compensation is determined in future air-crash cases, with victims arguing that awards should reflect actual economic loss, including income and future earning capacity, as well as inflation. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Thirty-eight years after an Indian Airlines flight crashed near Ahmedabad, killing 133 people, Air India has asked the Supreme Court to fast-track a hearing in a compensation dispute whose outcome could reshape how India compensates victims of air crashes.
 The apex court is scheduled to hear the plea on Monday, according to the cause list, after Air India filed its application on 1 October. At the heart of the dispute is a simple question: should families of air-crash victims continue to be compensated using formulas developed for road-accident victims under the Motor Vehicles Act, or should courts adopt a separate framework for aviation accidents?
 The outcome could shape how compensation is determined in future air-crash cases, with victims arguing that awards should reflect actual economic loss, including income and future earning capacity, as well as inflation. They also contend that compensation should account for airlines’ financial capacity and insurance cover, rather than being restricted by formulas developed for road accidents.
 "The decision could have implications beyond compensation for plane-crash victims, as it could shape the broader framework for consumer protection and how victims are compensated for harm," said Satyam Dwivedi, aviation law specialist and managing partner at DC Law Offices.
 Air India told the Supreme Court in September 2025 to keep the underlying question of law open for consideration in connected or future proceedings.
 The compensation dispute has been pending before the top court since 2010, after litigation arising from the 19 October 1988 crash travelled from the lower court in Ahmedabad to the Gujarat High Court and eventually to the Supreme Court.
 Emails seeking comments from Air India on Sunday morning and the Airports Authority of India (AAI) remained unanswered at the time of publication.
 Different framework 
 In written submissions filed in October 2025 and reviewed by Mint, the victims argued that compensation in an air-crash case should not be calculated using the Motor Vehicles Act framework used for road accidents. They said aviation accidents are fundamentally different because passengers have no control over an aircraft's operation or safety.
 Instead, they argued that compensation should account for the victim's actual economic loss, including income, future earning capacity and changes in earnings, as well as inflation.
The victims also argued that airlines are large, financially capable and insured enterprises, and that compensation in an air crash should therefore not be restricted by formulas developed for road accidents. They said the availability of insurance should also be considered while ensuring that victims receive full and just compensation.
 The plea also pointed to the 2010 Mangalore air-crash case, in which the Supreme Court applied principles under the Motor Vehicles Act to determine compensation. The victims, however, argued that the court did not specifically decide whether the MVA framework should apply to air-crash claims, leaving the issue open.
 Case could set a precedent 
 Lawyers say the case could ultimately have implications beyond compensation payable in the 1988 crash.
 ``This is a very important case, and the Supreme Court should use this opportunity under Article 142 to lay down standardised guidelines for compensation. You cannot put a different value on a person's life based on whether they travelled by air or road,'' said Dwivedi.
 Alay Razvi, managing partner at Accord Juris, said a more individualised approach could potentially increase compensation exposure in some cases.
 “If the Supreme Court requires a more individualised assessment of actual loss, compensation exposure may increase in cases involving young victims, high-income earners, professionals with demonstrable career growth or families with substantial financial dependency. Airlines may also face greater exposure where liability is shared with other parties but is not subject to an applicable statutory or convention-based limit,” Razvi said.
 Case history 
 The case dates back to 19 October 1988, when Indian Airlines Flight IC-113, operating from Mumbai to Ahmedabad, crashed while approaching Ahmedabad airport. The aircraft was carrying 135 people, including six crew members. Of these, 133 were killed, while two passengers survived, one of whom suffered substantial physical and mental disabilities.
 Families of the deceased and survivors filed 38 civil suits between 1989 and 1992 seeking compensation. The Ahmedabad City Civil Court decided the claims in 2002. The litigation then moved to the Gujarat High Court, which decided the appeals in 2009 and revised several awards.
 The dispute reached the Supreme Court in 2010. In April that year, the court recorded that the compensation determined against Indian Airlines had been deposited with the Ahmedabad City Civil Court, along with interest, while the Airports Authority of India had deposited 30% of the compensation. The court directed disbursement to claimants subject to them furnishing security other than a bank guarantee.
 Despite the passage of nearly four decades, the dispute has remained unresolved, prompting Air India to seek an early hearing before the Supreme Court.
 The hearing comes against the backdrop of the Air India crash last year that killed 260 people, with several related pleas concerning air safety and the investigation into the crash pending before the Supreme C

docs.title: Startups, OTT, real estate and more: Bollywood stars diversify their investments, build wealth beyond film salaries
docs.text:
Startups have become a popular choice. Stars increasingly want ownership in businesses rather than only promoting their products. Katrina Kaif launched Kay Beauty in partnership with Nykaa. Priyanka Chopra was an early investor in Bumble. Shraddha Kapoor has also backed brands and startups with hopes of future growth. Alia Bhatt built Ed-a-Mamma, a children’s clothing brand. Reliance later acquired a major stake in the company. She has also invested in Nykaa and Phool.co. Hrithik Roshan created HRX, which grew into a recognised activewear brand. Deepika Padukone invests through her company, Ka Enterprises. Her investments include Epigamia, BluSmart and Supertails. She has also launched the skincare brand 82°E. Property remains another favourite investment. Actors buy apartments, offices and land across different cities. These real estate assets can provide rent and an increase in value over time. In Mumbai, celebrities rent commercial properties to companies in Bandra, Andheri and Juhu. Kriti Sanon and her family reportedly earned significant profits by selling apartments in Andheri West. The Bachchan family has invested beyond Mumbai, including land in Pune and Ayodhya. Some actors have also invested in projects by Sri Lotus Developers. Sports ownership offers another route to building wealth. Shah Rukh Khan and Preity Zinta’s involvement with the IPL is a major example. Celebrities increasingly view these teams as assets that can grow over many years. SRK’s Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR) have won the IPL trophy thrice so far, trailing only behind Mumbai Indians and Chennai Super Kings. In July, the Knight Riders Group opened the Knight Riders Cricket Ground at the Fairplex in Pomona, California. Production houses allow actors to earn through ownership of films, web series, and other OTT content. For example, Anushka Sharma’s Clean Slate Filmz has produced Paatal Lok, a celebrated web series on Prime Video, and the Netflix film, Bulbbul. Alia Bhatt’s Eternal Sunshine Productions has co-produced the Netflix film, Darlings. It also co-produced Jigra, a theatrical release. Hrithik Roshan has recently launched HRXFilms. It has partnered with Prime Video. Its upcoming productions include Storm, a thriller series about five women, and Mess, an offbeat comedy. Shah Rukh Khan’s Red Chillies Entertainment and Farhan Akhtar’s Excel Entertainment produce a wide range of content. Income comes from streaming, television rights, overseas distribution and digital licensing. Such earnings can continue long after a film leaves cinemas. Some stars also invest in pre-IPO companies before they go public. Investors hope the company’s value will rise after its shares are listed. Reports suggest Aamir Khan and Ranbir Kapoor have explored such opportunities through advisers. These investments carry risks although successful companies can deliver significant returns. docs.title: Prime London Homes Are Increasingly on Frontlines of Extreme Weather
docs.text: (Bloomberg) -- More than a decade into a downturn caused by tax hikes, economic and political shocks, London’s high-end housing market has a new villain to contend with — intractable heat and flood risks. The assessment comes from Prime Purchase, the branch of Savills UK that represents property buyers in the top end of the real estate market. Guy Meacock, a director at Prime Purchase, says too many premium homes in the UK capital are ill-equipped to deal with the fallout of increasingly frequent extreme-weather shocks.“If London gets a reputation for having architecture that’s fundamentally not fit for purpose, then it’s not ludicrous to think that it will have as far reaching an impact on property values as anything else,” Meacock said in an interview.The development follows a summer during which London’s vulnerability to extreme heat was laid bare. Air conditioning remains a rarity, existing in less than 10% of properties countrywide. Even basic cooling features such as shutters and awnings have proved hard to get for some of London’s priciest real estate. More worrying still, perhaps, is the city’s flood risk as freak downpours fueled by climate change leave a growing number of properties — including those with luxury mega-basements — more difficult to insure. The concerns add to the list of headwinds facing the UK property market, which is already under pressure from high borrowing costs. Nationwide, house prices fell in August on an annual basis for the first time since 2023, according to the latest figures from Lloyds Banking Group. Prime central London property values are down 26% from a 2014 peak, according to Savills.Heat in particular is growing more relevant for some of London’s priciest boroughs, according to Meacock.He says international buyers are deterred not only by the lack of features to protect properties from weather-related risks, but also by what they perceive as fiendishly complex planning rules that would complicate any efforts to upgrade homes.“We are dealing with a lot of American buyers at the moment and the subject of air conditioning for them comes up every single time,” he said. Buyers are “staggered” to learn how unusual AC is in high-end London homes, so “your pool of potential properties suddenly shrinks.”Climate change is leaving a significant footprint on the UK capital. The government’s Environment Agency estimated in July that close to 320,000 London-based homes and businesses are now at “high risk” of surface-water flooding. In August, the office of the Mayor of London warned that extreme heat has become a “major and growing public health threat” in the city, with 86% of Londoners surveyed complaining of overheating in their homes. “The impact of climate change is having a profound effect on people’s mindset,” Meacock said. “And although it’s not yet having a really material impact on values, that is going to be the likely pathway.”He says London’s so-called golden postcodes, which are in the borough of Kensington and Chelsea, as well as parts of Westminster and its surrounding areas, are particularly vulnerable to shifts in sentiment from international buyers. With roughly half the buyers investing in such properties coming from outside the UK, sellers “can’t rely purely on domestic wealth, especially not with the current tax climate,” Meacock said.A major concern is the receding availability of insurance, which is tied to how likely the UK’s insurer of last resort — Flood Re — is to provide a backstop. The state-backed program applies only to homes built before 2009. In July, Flood Re unveiled a plan to ensure the program doesn’t disproportionately favor wealthy home owners, which means commercial insurers with multimillion-pound properties on their books won’t enjoy the same public support they used to. That change is expected to come into force from 2028. Flats in buildings with more than three properties also don’t qualify for Flood Re. Tracey Garrett, chief executive of the National Flood Forum, a nonprofit that advises homeowners, says the group’s helpline “often” hears from London residents who can’t get affordable coverage.“They just manage without flood insurance,” she said. That means they end up covering the cost of flood damage themselves. And even though “they may well be asset rich,” they’re not necessarily “day-to-day wealthy,” Garrett said.At insurance broker Howden Group, staff are already fielding calls from clients worried they won’t be able to sell high-end properties due to a lack of coverage. George Seatter, client director at Howden Private Clients, says he was called earlier this year by an agent representing the sellers of a £2 million property built in 2019 in Buckinghamshire, west of London. The property’s location close to the river Thames, combined with the fact that it’s not covered by Flood Re, initially left the buyers unable to find insurance. Commercial insurers “would have mapped the property, they’d have seen that it was in a perceived high-risk area for flood,” Seatter said. “They’d have looked at the fact that it was going to be a second home and built after 2009. They’d have known that they couldn’t cede it to Flood Re, and that would’ve been the end of the conversation.”In the event, Seatter says Howden was able to arrange a policy backed by a US insurer. Howden’s analysis of the site found that its precise location in relation to the river wasn’t a disqualifying risk. Seatter says insurers who invest in more detailed analyses are picking up business from competitors spooked by the broader trend.“From a flood risk perspective, we’re doing this all the time,” he said. “There are more and more properties that are in flood affected areas,” and as an insurer, if “you can then remove it from your books, so to speak, and you can pass on the cost to the client, almost, why wouldn’t you?”More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

docs.title: PF withdrawal done, pension forgotten? Why your EPS service record still needs to be transferred and how to do it
docs.text:
EPF and EPS are part of the same social security framework, but they serve different purposes. While EPF helps build a retirement corpus through contributions and interest and can also provide financial support during certain emergencies, EPS primarily tracks an employee’s eligible pensionable service. Generally, a longer eligible service period can result in the employee receiving higher pension benefits after they retire. When an employee withdraws their EPF balance, their EPS service history does not automatically get transferred. Hence, when you switch jobs, it is important to ensure that your pensionable service from previous employment is properly linked to your current EPF account. This matters because EPS eligibility is based on your total eligible pensionable service. Employees generally need at least 10 years of eligible service to qualify for a monthly pension. If your service records are not properly carried forward, your employment history could appear incomplete. The EPS contribution rate is 8.33% of the monthly wages, which is diverted directly from the employer's total 12% contribution to the employee's EPF account. An employee does not have to contribute towards EPS. Even if you have already withdrawn your entire EPF balance but later realise that your EPS service history was not carried forward, you are not without options. An employee can transfer their service record later after submitting Form 13 through the EPFO member portal and complete the transfer process. Several common errors such as incorrect personal details, UAN records or KYC information can delay the transfer process of EPS service. An incorrect or missing date of exit in the previous employer's records can also create problems when employees try to transfer their service history. Before submitting Form 13, employees should check that their employment and personal details are accurate and up to date. An outdated date of exit can be particularly problematic. Employees should first ask their former employer to correct the record. If the employer does not update it, they can also do it themselves now on the EPFO portal. Follow the given steps to change or update your job leaving date: Step 1: Log in to the official EPFO member portal using your Universal Account Number (UAN) and password. Step 2: Once you are in, navigate to the Manage tab on the home page and click on the Mark Exit option. Step 4: Select the appropriate reason for leaving and enter the correct date of exit, as per your official employment records and the month of your last PF contribution. Step 5: After you have entered the required details, proceed with Aadhaar-based OTP verification and submit the request. As the process involves authentication, the member must ensure that their mobile number is linked with Aadhaar and in their possession at the time. If the online facility is not allowing you to make the required correction, then you have to approach your former employer for help. If they fail to respond within a few days or weeks, then you also have the option to file a complaint through EPFO's grievance mechanism. She has pursued her graduation from St. Joseph’s University, Bengaluru in a multi-disciplinary course. Her majors included Journalism, International Relations, peace and conflict studies.

docs.title: Are fliers guinea pigs for aviation authorities?
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Are fliers guinea pigs for aviation authorities?
 Shashi Shekhar 4 min read 5 Oct 2026, 06:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 It’s clear that new effective norms for fliers and pilots can’t be ignored any longer. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 It was 24 March 2015. Germanwings Airbus Flight 9525 departed from Barcelona, Spain, the world’s soccer capital. It was carrying 144 passengers and six crew members. Thirty minutes later, flying over the snow-capped French Alps, everything looked fine. The flight was cruising at its usual altitude when the plane nosedived, and before the shocked passengers could understand anything, the huge Airbus crashed into a peak. All 150 on board died a horrific death.
 The aviation world went into a tizzy. An investigation was launched immediately. What French Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety (BEA) investigators found was chilling. According to their report, the 27-year-old co-pilot Andreas Lubitz crashed the plane deliberately. He had been suffering from depression. This was why, when the captain went to the washroom during the flight, he bolted the cockpit door from the inside. Then he took control of the plane and turned its direction downwards and accelerated. Cockpit voice recorder suggested the captain had tried hard to open the cockpit door but failed. His efforts went in vain, resulting in the terrible tragedy.
 Those unaware should know that after the 9/11 terror attack on Twin Towers in New York in 2001, cockpit doors were reconfigured so that they couldn’t be opened from the outside.
 After the incident, Indian and global aviation authorities mandated that two people be present in the cockpit at all times.
 Last year, Air India’s massive Boeing 787 Dreamliner crashed moments after it took off from Ahmedabad airport, killing 260 people. Initial investigations revealed that the fuel switches were shut. Aircraft manufacturer Boeing conducted its own probe and gave the plane a clean chit. It didn’t name anyone but the indication was clear. Either the pilot was responsible for the crash or it was a sabotage.
 Boeing investigates crashes involving its aircraft around the world and, more often than not, finds no fault with its own product. This tendency is not unique to Boeing; multinational companies, from Boeing to Union Carbide, have often displayed the same instinct.
 After the Ahmedabad crash, debate raged over the critical switch design, pilots’ regular training and mandatory mental health checks. But some lessons faded from collective memory. Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv is a glaring reminder of that lapse .
 It is alleged that the Omani pilot attacked and grievously wounded Indian pilot Smit Machchhar with an axe. Showing exemplary courage, Machchhar not only tried to restrain the attacker but also managed to open the cockpit door. Where did the protocols put in place after the 2015 incident disappear? Why weren’t pilot antecedents checked? Is this what global airlines and their regulators have learnt after losing hundreds of people from the French Alps to Ahmedabad?
 It is heartening that Machchhar is receiving global recognition. Israel wants to confer its highest honour on him, while there have also been calls in India for him to be awarded the Ashoka Chakra. A stoic hero, what he thought of his act became clear in a phone conversation with Prime Minister Narendra Modi , when he said he was determined not to let a single passenger die.
 It’s clear that the blessings and good wishes of all the 174 passengers on flight FZ1073 will remain with him for life.
 Omani authorities have identified the attacker as their citizen. Details of his birth, education, his friends circle and the motive for such an act are not clear. However, a US daily has claimed that the attacker’s name is Hammam Al Hammami and he was banned in Oman for his extremist views. Is it a coincidence that Germanwings pilot Lubitz was also able to hide his depression and no-fly recommendations from the authorities? A repeat by Hammami shows that the aviation authorities are beset by outdated thinking in the age of modern communications.
 Are fliers guinea pigs for aviation authorities? How long can we keep flying on wings and a prayer? This incident has once again proved that the threat to planes is present in cockpits, too. Not only planes, helicopters with their payload of tonnes of fuel can become a deadly weapon over densely populated areas. 9/11 is its biggest example. It’s clear that new effective norms for fliers and pilots can’t be ignored any longer. We also need a serious global discourse on the spread of hate-mongering, which is increasingly afflicting even the educated elite. The Omani pilot is the latest example.
 Shashi Shekhar is editor-in-chief, Hindustan. Views are personal.

docs.text:
Lounge 
 ‘Digger’ review: Tom Cruise climate crisis film is trial by satire
 Uday Bhatia 3 min read 4 Oct 2026, 03:47 PM IST 
 Summary
 Alejandro G. Iñárritu's ‘Digger’, starring Tom Cruise as an oil tycoon, is a wild punt that never comes close to delivering on its political and cultural criticisms 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 In the run-up to Digger’s release, a stray theory caught on that Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s film might be a stealth musical. It was a sizeable enough rumour that the studio actually issued a disclaimer that it wasn't. I was reminded of this at the end of an elaborate sequence, the centrepiece of the film in many ways, in which oil tycoon Digger Rockwell (Tom Cruise) is addressing a European Parliament of sorts. He starts off conciliatory and ends up combative, enraging his audience to the point that they stop yelling and start singing “blah blah blah blah blah”.
 Even when there’s music, Digger is an aggressively unmusical film. It’s all stops and starts, lurches and stumbles, Dutch angles and extreme closeups. Iñárritu and his longtime cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki give everything a ghostly white pallor; with a decrepit, balding Tom Cruise in almost every scene, it feels like the ghost of capitalisms past. Iñárritu’s Oscar-winning Birdman was scored and performed to perpetual aggressive rhythms, yet had no intrinsic rhythm of its own. Digger , on the other hand, feels purposely ungainly, world-is-ending vaudeville on a $160 million budget.
 On one of Digger’s many oil rigs in Greenland, a methane leak results in an explosion that causes a large ice shelf to break off. The magnate is informed by Nirav Ganesh (Riz Ahmed), a scientist in his employ, that ‘Judy’ is on a collision course with Europe, though there’s a chance it might be carried away from land and melt in the sea. US President Compson (John Goodman) is summoned and there’s a crisis meeting with the Digger, Ganesh, the chiefs of staff, the vice president (Michael Stuhlbarg) and the president’s priest. Their decision, in essence, is to do nothing: it’ll either be a near miss and no one will care, or it’ll be Europe’s problem.
 This is Strangelovian satire in both tenor and staging, but with all the edge of a butter knife. There's nothing shocking about the film's political scenarios—reality is simply moving too fast now for this kind of knowing farce. One of Digger’s many headaches is his sick (and weirdly animatronic) cat, an overwrought metaphor for a world that’s just about clinging on. In the reality of this film, the climate crisis had reached the point of frequent catastrophe. Digger is one of the root causes, unchecked, unrepentant, unscientific, a fitting archvillain for the Trump era (even if it’s set years after our present).
 (spoilers ahead) 
 For the second time this fortnight, I have no choice but to discuss a major plot development, both for what it says about the film’s ambitions and how it fits into Iñárritu’s oeuvre. After the situation room meeting, Digger and Compson continue talking in another room. As they gaze out over a green vista, they're interrupted by a voice calling for better timing on a falling tree. We're now shown that we’ve been watching the dress rehearsal of an ambitious stage production, a play called ‘Fossil Fools’. Digger is being played by an actor called Curtis Markson, who’s bristling against the over-the-top spin he’s been asked to put on the character. At least the fake cat makes sense.
 Here, at least, is proper risk-taking. But as this parallel plot progresses, it becomes clear that it has little emotional resonance with the play. Rather, Iñárritu opts for the most literal-minded connection: Curtis’ daughter is on a flight that’s gone missing due to extreme weather. It’s a baffling decision; the scenes from ‘Fossil Fools’ are so much worse now that we’re aware of Curtis’ (and Iñárritu’s?) contempt for them. There’s a lot of Birdman in Digger : the woozy, meandering camera of Lubezki, the self-reflexive games, pity for the poor artist stuck in the maw of commerce (the reveal about the play’s financing is one of the film’s better dark jokes). The difference is the gimmick then was the one-shot illusion, and now it’s Cruise.
 You have to go back to the mid-2000s to find Cruise in non-franchise, non-blockbuster parts. Digger Rockwell is the most transparent movie-star-wants-to-be-taken-seriously-again role: big accent, tons of makeup, winding monologues. Is it a good performance? Inasmuch as the film makes it difficult to concentrate on anything, I don’t think it is. I felt nothing for Digger, neither pity nor contempt nor grudging admiration, and I’m betting the film was hoping to elicit all three. In the days since the film’s release, there’s a small but vocal minority—including some of Iñárritu’s director friends—arguing that the problem is the film community’s diminished appetite for risk. It’s the easiest excuse: the viewer isn’t ready. The film goes out on a limb, so it must be relevant. Prescient. Ahead of its time. Blah blah blah blah blah.
 ‘ Digger ’ is in theatres .

FPIs most bearish in 2 months; rapid turnaround unlikely: Analysts
 Analysts say low FII long-short readings often trigger short-covering, but a sustained rally looks unlikely amid crude, bond-yield and geopolitical pressures
 premium 
 Foreign funds are selling index futures or have shorted the market, showing low confidence in the growth prospects of Indian stocks
 Kairavi Lukka Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 04 2026 | 10:16 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Overseas investors have turned the most bearish on Indian markets in more than two months, as weak global macroeconomic signals have made Dalal Street investments less attractive. Analysts said that while such low levels of foreign investor positioning often trigger short-covering rallies, a sustained recovery appears unlikely this time.
 Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are either selling index futures or holding short positions, signalling low confidence in the growth prospects of Indian equities. Funds typically cover short positions when the risk-reward equation changes. However, the US-Iran conflict, higher 10-year US Treasury yields and rising Brent crude prices are keeping foreign investors cautious.
 The FII Long-Short Ratio, a measure of their long positions relative to short positions in index futures on the NSE, fell to just 8 per cent at Thursday’s close, its lowest level since July 23. Equity markets were closed on October 2 for Gandhi Jayanti. The Long-Short Ratio is considered a sentiment indicator, with lower readings indicating greater bearishness among FIIs.
 The Nifty ended 0.9 per cent lower at 22,421.95 on Thursday and has declined 14.25 per cent so far this year. Foreign investors have consequently pulled out ₹2.69 trillion from Indian equities, according to the latest NSDL data. 
 Vipin Kumar, AVP, derivatives and technical research at Globe Capital Market, said the short-term chart structure is in oversold territory, with the Nifty reaching key structural support levels in the 22,180-21,740 spot zone.
 “Meanwhile, the Long-Short ratio has dropped to extreme lows, indicating that a potential bounce-back rally toward the 22,800-22,850 spot zone cannot be ruled out at this juncture,” he said. “However, given elevated crude oil prices driven by volatile geopolitical conditions and rising US Treasury yields, the chances of sustainability at higher levels remain low.”
 Any sharp upside is therefore likely to face selling pressure on rallies, Kumar said.
 A Business Standard analysis showed that FII short positions have remained below the 20 per cent mark on 159 of 182 trading days so far in 2026, and below 10 per cent on 46 occasions.
 “FII long positions have remained below 10 per cent for some time, but unlike in the past, this has not triggered a recovery. The macro factors behind these short positions remain unchanged, with rising bond yields and crude prices, along with a weaker rupee, providing little incentive for FIIs to cover their shorts,” said Chandan Taparia, head, technical and derivatives research, Motilal Oswal Financial Services.
 Selling pressure remains 
 Taparia said that while the Nifty is now deeply oversold, a sustained recovery may remain elusive until fresh positive triggers emerge.
 “Given the current risk-reward, further shorting may also be less attractive. In the near term, the Nifty could remain range bound between 22,200 and 22,750, with any bounces meeting with selling pressure,” he said.
 Kumar of Globe Capital also said that the formation of a solid reversal pattern or a stable base around these support levels would be critical for restoring bullish momentum.

Sebi CAS review draws over 20K responses; traders resist VWAP shift
 FIA, a global body of traders and exchanges, favours the 30-minute CTS-VWAP option and continuous trading till 3:30 pm
 premium 
 With the consultation now closed, Sebi is expected to examine the large volume of feedback before finalising the revised CAS framework (Photo: Reuters)
 Khushboo Tiwari Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 04 2026 | 10:06 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has received over 20,000 comments on its consultation paper on the closing auction session (CAS).
 And, traders as well as market participants sought continuation of the last 30-minute continuous trading session (CTS) volume-weighted average price (VWAP) method before any shift to a blended framework.
 With the consultation now closed, Sebi is expected to examine the large volume of feedback before finalising the revised CAS framework.
 The unusually high response comes as the market regulator reviews the CAS mechanism introduced for stocks with derivatives contracts from August 3 — which also resulted in sharp decline in the trading volumes in futures and options (F&O).
 Sebi’s review came after uproar from the trading community. Further, the regulator also saw certain instances of alleged manipulation in the window.
 Sebi's consultation had proposed two alternatives for determining expiry-day settlement prices. They are a blended VWAP incorporating trades during the final 30 minutes of CTS and the 10-minute CAS, or continuation of the CTS-only VWAP for at least a year before considering a transition to the blended methodology.
 Feedback from traders, brokers, and other participants has favoured the latter, with participants arguing that the existing 30-minute VWAP is familiar, transparent and operationally well understood.
 They also said that retaining it temporarily would allow CAS to develop its own liquidity and price-discovery characteristics before its trades are incorporated into derivatives settlement.
 The Futures Industry Association (FIA), a global body with members from exchanges, clearing firms and trading firms across countries, in its response to Sebi submitted on Saturday, strongly disagreed with the immediate adoption of blended VWAP and backed CTS VWAP as the interim methodology.
 It said the variable weights assigned to CTS and CAS would only be known after the auction, even though participants would have to execute the CTS portion beforehand.
 “This difficulty in tracking the settlement price has direct consequences for participants seeking to maintain their total exposure through expiry. These include funds using index futures to hedge their portfolios, arbitrageurs whose derivatives positions are perfectly hedged with underlying stocks, and long-term investors who initially obtained exposure through derivatives for liquidity reasons,” it noted in its submissions to Sebi.
 FIA also pointed to lower trading volumes observed during CAS. It recommended that any future move to blended VWAP be conditional on a clearly-defined liquidity trigger demonstrating that the auction has sufficient liquidity to be incorporated into derivatives settlement. It also called for further consultation with market participants before any change.
 On market timings, FIA and several other traders backed Sebi's Option A — extending continuous trading in CAS stocks to 3:30 pm, followed by the auction, with derivatives trading until 3:45 pm. They noted that the longer continuous session would support price discovery and align the derivatives close more closely with completion of the cash-market closing process.
 FIA, however, opposed Sebi's proposal to stop disseminating the indicative index value (IIV) during CAS.
 It said IIVs provide market participants with a real-time reference for understanding how closing prices are forming and can assist surveillance by allowing futures prices to be compared with the implied value of the underlying basket.
 Removing the information could reduce transparency without necessarily addressing manipulation risks, it argued.
 Sebi's consultation also proposed allowing unexecuted Iceberg orders to enter CAS after being converted into fully displayed normal limit orders, and shortening the transition between continuous trading and CAS to up to one minute.
 The regulator had also proposed prohibiting cancellation of limit orders placed beyond 1 per cent range of the reference price during CAS. But it permitted only price improving modifications to such orders.
 Sebi officials had earlier noted that the VWAP method was prone to manipulation.
