'Nifty's mcap composition causes it to trail broader earnings growth'
 Abakkus' Sunil Singhania says India's changing economic structure could shift growth towards newer industries and smaller companies
 premium 
 From left: Sunil Singhania, Founder, Abakkus Asset Manager, and Vaibhav Chugh, CEO, Abakkus Mutual Fund.
 Abhishek Kumar Mumbai 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 04 2026 | 10:43 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 India’s economic composition is changing and the next leg of growth will not necessarily be driven by the same set of companies, says Sunil Singhania, Founder, Abakkus Asset Manager. In an in-person interview with Abhishek Kumar in Mumbai, Singhania and Vaibhav Chugh, CEO of Abakkus Mutual Fund, share their views on the market correction, the evolving investment landscape and factors driving MF business growth. Edited Excerpts:
 Equity markets have remained under pressure over the past two years, with volatility intensifying in the past week. What’s causing the extended time and price correction? 
 Sunil: 2020-2024 was an exceptional period as the equity market generated nearly 6 years’ worth of return in a 4-year period. So, the last two years have partly been a normalisation of the long-term return trend.
 There have also been several headwinds. In 2024, economic growth weakened significantly. Then there were factors like global AI trade which led to money mostly flowing into markets such as China, Korea, Taiwan and Japan. Trump tariffs and the ongoing West Asia conflict were also a setback for the market.
 However, domestically, things look much better now. Growth has recovered, supported by government measures like income tax and GST cuts. The RBI also infused substantial liquidity into the domestic economy. 
 But, the elevated oil prices continue to weigh on the market. The question is how long the war premium on the oil prices will remain. If that premium eases, it would be a significant positive for India.
 Can the weaker monsoons add to the pressure? 
 Sunil: The monsoon is currently below normal. However, the positive aspect is that sowing is still around normal levels. The more important factor is the output of the winter crop. If we have a very dry or hot winter, agricultural production could be affected.
 Abakkus Mutual Fund has scaled up quickly since its launch in December 2025. What would you attribute this to? 
 Vaibhav: There are several factors. First is the experience Abakkus has built on the alternatives side over the last eight to nine years, along with our Founder Sunil Singhania's experience of over three decades as an investment manager. The second is the effort we have put into communicating who we are, how we manage money and, importantly, how we manage risk. At the same time, we have been building relationships with distributors across the country.
 Where has the growth primarily come from? How does the mix look between direct and regular? And which channels within regular contribute the most? 
 Vaibhav: Majority of our business is distribution-led. Within that, there is an interesting aspect: A lot of distributors are also giving money through registered investment advisors (RIAs) or platforms. So, while it may appear under a particular category, the underlying investment may actually be advised through a platform. Overall, the business is fairly diversified with the regular plan business coming from across channels including wealth managers, banks, national distributors and individual MF distributors.
 Have these market conditions created opportunities for stock picking? Which market cap segment is most attractive currently? 
 Sunil: Stock picking is always difficult. There are some pockets of the market that are completely neglected, while in other areas valuations have risen sharply. In some companies, price movements appear to be driven largely by Fomo-led (fear-of-missing-out-led) retail participation and momentum-driven buying. Overall, the market is transforming and the traditional large-cap, mid-cap and small-cap framework needs to be looked at differently.
 Nifty currently consists of many good companies, but not all firms that have been successful historically will necessarily be the fastest-growing companies in the future. IT services may not be able to grow at high rates indefinitely. Consumer staples and oil and gas companies also have structural growth limitations.
 At the same time, most emerging industries are currently in the mid-cap and small-cap segments. As a result, the composition of the Nifty can cause it to trail the broader corporate earnings growth.
 Which sectors do you see participating in India's next phase of growth? 
 Sunil: India's economic composition is changing. The first trillion dollars of India's economy took around 60 years. During that period, public-sector enterprises played a major role because of the structure of the economy after independence. Steel, aluminium, power, coal, oil and gas, public-sector banks and other traditional industries were important.
 Between $1 trillion and $4 trillion, private-sector banks, pharmaceuticals, IT services and consumption became much more important. As India moves from $4 trillion towards $8 trillion, the composition could change again.
 In healthcare, instead of only generic pharmaceutical companies, we could see opportunities across Contract Development and Manufacturing Organisations (CDMOs), drug discovery, hospitals, medical technology (medtech), and diagnostics companies. In energy, alongside thermal power, there could be greater participation from solar, EVs and battery storage. Similarly, instead of only IT services, we could see platform companies, data centres and semiconductors.

docs.title: 20%+ profit growth, no debt: 2 stocks riding India’s $3.6 bn dental boom
docs.text: India’s dental industry is moving beyond clinics and hospitals towards a larger manufacturing opportunity in dental materials, consumables, prostheses and laboratory products. Grand View Research estimates India’s dental equipment and consumables market generated USD 2.09 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach USD 3.62 billion by 2030, implying a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.6% during 2025-30. Importantly, dental consumables were the largest product segment in 2024, making this the most relevant pool for Indian manufacturers rather than the broader dental-services market. The consumables opportunity becomes even more significant when viewed separately. Grand View Research estimates India’s dental consumables market at USD 1.73 billion in 2025, with revenue projected to reach USD 3.63 billion by 2033, representing a 9.7% CAGR from 2026-33. Dental implants were the largest segment in 2025, while dental biomaterials are projected to be the fastest-growing segment. There is also a sizeable laboratory manufacturing opportunity. The opportunity is therefore not restricted to imported equipment. India is building domestic capabilities across dental materials, biomaterials, prostheses, aligners and laboratory products. This is where manufacturing-led listed companies such as Laxmi Dental and Prevest DenPro fit into the expanding dental value chain. #1 Laxmi Dental: Where Laboratory Scale Meets Digital Dentistry Laxmi Dental Limited operates across dental laboratory solutions, aligners and paediatric dental products. Its largest business is dental laboratory solutions, operated primarily through Illusion Dental Lab, which provides customised dental prostheses such as crowns and bridges. Its aligner business includes Illusion Aligners and Taglus, with Taglus manufacturing thermoforming sheets, 3D-printing resins, machines and accessories used in orthodontic applications. Kids-e-Dental is its paediatric dental business and serves more than 15 countries. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Q1 FY27: Growth Came From the Core Engine Laxmi Dental reported its highest-ever quarterly revenue in Q1 FY27, with consolidated revenue from operations of ₹74.70 crore, up 13.9% year on year (YoY) and 1% quarter on quarter (QoQ). Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased 20.6% to ₹14.36 crore, taking EBITDA margin to 19.2%, while profit after tax (PAT), after the share of profit/loss from joint ventures, rose 23.8% to ₹10.32 crore. PAT margin improved to 13.8% from 12.7% in Q1 FY26. The quality of this growth is more important than the headline number. Laboratory revenue increased to ₹50.28 crore from ₹44.59 crore, while laboratory revenue excluding scanner sales grew 23.5%. International laboratory operations grew 37.4%. Aligner Solutions revenue increased to ₹24.17 crore from ₹18.73 crore, while its segment result rose to ₹6.53 crore from ₹2.28 crore. Within the aligner segment, Bizdent and Vedia grew 27.8% and 29.3%, respectively, during Q1 FY27. If the higher-margin aligner business continues to grow faster than laboratory solutions, it could gradually lift consolidated profitability even if overall revenue growth remains moderate. The Scanner Question Is More Important Than Scanner Sales Scanner revenue fell to ₹2.2 crore in Q1 FY27 from ₹5.9 crore a year earlier. However, management has consistently described scanners as a strategic enabler of digital dentistry rather than simply a hardware revenue stream. The issue is therefore not whether scanner revenue grows every quarter. It is whether scanner deployment produces a larger pool of laboratory and aligner revenue over time. The company's earlier disclosures indicate that scanner sales typically carry lower margins, while the laboratory and aligner businesses have stronger economics. Q1 FY27's higher gross margin of 78.6% therefore benefited from the lower contribution of scanners. Revenue increased from ₹239 crore in FY25 to ₹278 crore in FY26, but operating profit increased by only ₹1 crore, while PAT declined. FY26 showed that revenue expansion alone did not guarantee higher earnings, making operating leverage the key metric to track. ALSO READ5 Fundamentally Strong Stocks Trading Below Historical Valuations Palghar Could Change the Economics The company is moving towards an owned manufacturing facility at Palghar, Maharashtra, alongside three new support facilities in India. That could change more than Laxmi Dental’s capacity. An owned facility could give the company greater control over manufacturing, automation and operating costs as volumes scale. If Laxmi can ramp utilisation without a proportionate increase in employee and laboratory costs, Palghar could improve operating leverage and support higher volumes over time. The key variables to watch are commissioning, utilisation and incremental revenue generation, because these will determine whether the expansion translates into better returns on capital. Debt Is No Longer the Immediate Constraint Laxmi had nil consolidated borrowings as of 31 March 2026, following repayment of its remaining term loan during FY26. This gives the company room to fund expansion without starting FY27 with conventional debt on the balance sheet. However, debt-free does not mean capital-light. The company is investing in machinery, facilities, digital systems and international operations. The more useful measure will therefore be free cash flow after expansion spending and the return generated on the additional capital. docs.title: Rs 588 Bn exports, 90%+ rally: 2 stocks riding India’s aircraft-parts boom
docs.text: India’s aircraft-component manufacturing opportunity is expanding rapidly even before the country begins producing complete commercial aircraft at scale. A Frost & Sullivan analysis estimates India’s commercial-aircraft manufacturing market at ₹164.21 billion in 2026, up from ₹130.51 billion in 2024. It is projected to reach ₹257.09 billion by 2030, implying an 11.96% Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) during 2024–2030. The export opportunity is even larger. Ministry of Commerce data cited in an industry report shows India’s exports of aircraft and space parts jumped to ₹588.38 billion in FY25, from ₹269.03 billion in FY24 and ₹119.37 billion in FY19. This indicates a fast expansion of India’s participation in global aerospace supply chains. India’s expanding airline fleet backs demand. As of June 30, 2025, major Indian airlines had orders for 2,026 aircraft, according to data supplied by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) to Parliament. Of these, 385 aircraft had already been imported by that date, leaving a substantial pipeline of aircraft to be inducted over the coming years. The scale of these orders is expected to support long-term demand across India's aerospace supply chain, including aerostructures, precision-machined components, electrical systems and assemblies. This creates a sizable opportunity for specialised suppliers serving global Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and Tier-1 aerospace companies, including Dynamatic Technologies and Aequs. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 Dynamatic Technologies: From Detail Parts to Major Aerostructures Dynamatic Technologies operates across aerospace, hydraulics, metallurgy and security applications. Its aerospace business is conducted through Dynamatic-Oldland Aerospace and covers detail parts, sub-assemblies, assemblies and major assemblies. The company says its aerospace infrastructure delivers more than 800 aircraft shipsets annually and has manufactured more than 10,000 detail parts. Its customer base includes Airbus, Boeing, Bell Helicopter, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Dassault Aviation, Deutsche Aircraft and Prestwick Aerosystems, while its United Kingdom (UK) operations also serve Airbus UK, Boeing, GE Aviation, GKN Aerospace, Lockheed Martin, Spirit AeroSystems UK and AgustaWestland. Q1 FY27 Shows Operating Leverage, but Foreign Exchange (FX) Matters Dynamatic reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹424.81 crore in Q1 FY27, up 14.5% year-on-year (YoY) but down 1.9% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ). Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 45.9% YoY to ₹55.11 crore, taking the margin to 13%, while Profit After Tax (PAT) increased 92.9% YoY to ₹20.79 crore. The company said Q1 FY27 revenue would have grown 3.9% YoY on a constant-currency basis after removing a ₹39.26 crore favourable foreign-exchange impact. Constant-currency EBITDA would have been ₹49.97 crore instead of ₹55.11 crore. This means the underlying operating improvement was still positive, but headline growth overstated the underlying volume and execution momentum. Aerospace Is the Highest-Margin Business Aerospace revenue increased 17% YoY to ₹202.25 crore and represented 48% of Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue. Aerospace EBITDA rose 20.5% to ₹48.19 crore, while the EBITDA margin improved to 23.8% from 23.1% a year earlier and 20.7% in Q4 FY26. EBIT margin also increased to 17.8% from 16.8% in Q1 FY26. The company attributed the growth to execution across commercial aerospace and defence programmes and the ramp-up of detail-part programmes at Dynamatic Manufacturing Limited. The Airbus A220 doors programme also progressed during the quarter. The Rest of Dynamatic Still Matters Hydraulics generated ₹116.04 crore in Q1 FY27 revenue, up 9.4% YoY, while EBITDA rose 302.8% to ₹14.46 crore and the margin improved to 12.5% from 3.4%. Management attributed the improvement to product-mix optimisation and benefits from UK restructuring. Metallurgy generated ₹106.31 crore, up 15.7% YoY, with EBITDA rising 132.7% to ₹3.98 crore and the margin improving to 3.7%. This diversification changes how readers should view Dynamatic. It is not a pure-play aerospace stock. Aerospace provides the strongest margin profile and the largest revenue contribution, while the improvement in hydraulics and metallurgy is also supporting consolidated earnings. Consequently, future stock performance will depend on both aerospace execution and whether the non-aerospace businesses sustain their margin recovery. Five-Year Numbers Show Earnings Volatility ParticularsFY22FY23FY24FY25FY26Sales (₹ in crores)1,2531,3161,4291,4041,621Operating Profit (₹ in crores)172184162161186Net Profit (₹ in crores)15431224332Source: Screener.in Over FY22-FY26, revenue grew at a modest 6.7% CAGR, and earnings followed a far less predictable path. The wide swings in net profit show that revenue growth alone has not produced a stable earnings base, making the durability of the recent margin improvement more important than the pace of topline growth. ALSO READRs 50,000 Cr BESS push: 3 stocks targeting 37 GWh of India’s storage boom Debt Is Improving, but It Has Not Disappeared As of June 30, 2026, Dynamatic's total debt stood at ₹527.26 crore, compared with ₹479.97 crore a year earlier. Cash and cash equivalents were ₹54.12 crore, resulting in net debt of ₹473.14 crore. Including lease liabilities, overall debt stood at ₹577.42 crore. Net debt/Last Twelve Months (LTM) EBITDA improved to 2.4x from 2.5x at March 2026 and 2.8x at June 2025, while interest coverage improved to 2.4x. The improvement is encouraging, but leverage remains relevant because aerospace expansion requires continued investment. docs.title: Rs 50,000 Cr BESS push: 3 stocks targeting 37 GWh of India’s storage boom
docs.text: India’s Battery Energy Storage System opportunity is moving into a much larger phase. The government has approved ₹50,000 crore for deploying 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) under the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III scheme. The broader ₹1.86 lakh crore programme is designed to support the evacuation of up to 135 GW of renewable energy by FY33. The broader programme also includes ₹1.36 lakh crore for intra-state transmission systems, creating opportunities for transmission companies. We previously covered three transmission stocks positioned to benefit from this spending. Macro Context: How Green Energy Corridor Phase-III Fuels Grid Stability But the opportunity is moving beyond transmission. As solar and wind energy capacity expands, BESS is becoming critical to manage intermittency, meet peak-hour demand and supply power during non-solar hours. The ₹50,000 crore allocation for BESS could accelerate investments across the storage ecosystem. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now We previously covered three stocks with some of the highest ongoing BESS capacity in India. Building on that theme, this article looks at three other companies positioned to benefit from the BESS opportunity. #1 Pace Digitek Pace Digitek operates across Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) and Operations & Maintenance within the Telecom & ICT, Energy and BESS sectors. The BESS platform is a primary driver of the company's growth. It links in-house component and container manufacturing with turnkey project execution and post-commissioning maintenance. BESS Integration Engine: Why In-House Manufacturing Anchors Pace Digitek's 10 GWh Push The company operates a manufacturing capacity of 5 GWh through two 2.5 GWh production lines. Pace Digitek is adding another 5 GWh manufacturing line, which is expected to become operational by the third quarter of FY27. This will bring the company's total capacity to 10 GWh. BESS products yield an EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortisation) margin of 13% to 15%. Import Substitution: How ₹300-Cr Container Capex Unlocks a 2,000-Unit Annual Run Rate Pace Digitek has set up its own container manufacturing facility to substitute imported containers. Production was scheduled to start in September 2026. It will address a bottleneck in domestic supply. The company is investing ₹300 crore across Phase 1, Phase 2, and container fabrication. Pace holds an executable energy order book of ₹8,453 crore (5.10 GWh executable visibility) as of June 30. The company has manufactured and supplied over 300 grid-scale BESS containers. At full 10 GWh capacity, output will reach 2,000 containers per year. It is ramping up production, which is up from over 90 containers supplied in Q1FY27 to a target of 210 containers in Q2FY27. A BESS container is a ready-made, plug-and-play energy system container. As of June 30 2026, the company held an order book of ₹10,803 crore. Management has guided for revenue of ₹3,200-3,400 crore for FY27. Following a Q1FY27 revenue of ₹555 crore, execution is expected to step up sharply to ₹900-1,000 crore in Q2. Management further plans to scale revenue to ₹4,000-₹4,200 crore by FY28. Pace Digitek: Balancing High-Volume Capex Against Blended Margin Pressure Financially, the company's revenue grew 51.3% year-on-year to ₹555.4 crore in Q1FY27. This was primarily driven by the Energy business, which contributed 79.5% of revenue due to project execution across BESS and renewable energy deployments. EBITDA increased by 7.5% to ₹86.1 crore in Q1FY27, as margin fell by 630 bps to 15.5%. Net profit grew 14.3% to ₹62.5 crore. The energy business yields a lower margin (13-15% product EBITDA / 7-10% EPC) than the telecom business (20.5%). Due to the telecom division's revenue contribution declining to 20.5%, the overall blended operating margin contracted. Pace Digitek Share Price #2 Vikram Solar Vikram Solar is a major Indian solar photovoltaic (PV) module manufacturer. It currently has an operational module manufacturing capacity of 15.5 GW. The company is consolidating its manufacturing supply chain into a single contiguous hub at Gangaikondan, Tamil Nadu. In the BESS segment, the company designs, manufactures, assembles, and deploys energy storage systems. ALSO READNew Rs 1.86 lakh cr Green Corridor scheme: 3 stocks riding the transmission boom From PV Modules to PowerHive: Why Vikram Solar Is Stacking a 15 GWh BESS Moat The company's core offerings include Utility-Scale Storage Solutions. The business has already executed its first 20 megawatt-hour (MWh) utility-scale order. Vikram Solar has entered the commercial and industrial (C&I) and utility-scale energy storage solutions sector through its newly launched brand, "PowerHive." The BESS business complements Vikram Solar's solar PV manufacturing. By offering battery storage with solar modules, it provides complete, dispatchable clean energy solutions. The company aims to build a 15 GWh integrated cell manufacturing and assembly ecosystem by FY30. It plans to capture full in-house value across the storage value chain. Backwards Integration Timeline: How Ingot-to-LFP Capex Aims to Insulate Supply by FY30 An automated module facility with a capacity of 6 GW was commissioned in June 2026. The 9 GW solar cell facility plans to roll out its first cell in Q4FY27. Management projects 40-50% utilisation for FY28. In-house manufacturing and assembly operations are currently under construction. It is setting up a 15 GWh integrated BESS ecosystem. docs.title: 2.7X profit, 3X dividend growth, 3.7% yield: Is this PSU bank still undervalued?
docs.text: Welcome to the latest edition of Dividend Hunter. In recent weeks, we have analysed companies where strong cash flows could translate into consistent dividends. In our previous edition, we covered a public sector undertakingNBFC that delivered a 3.8% dividend yield. This week, in our 'Dividend Hunter' series, we are discussing a fast-growing and leading Indian public sector bank that has a market capitalisation of ₹1,19,365 crore as of October 1, 2026. In FY26, its total business crossed the ₹30 lakh crore milestone. Additionally, it recorded its highest-ever annual net profit of ₹20,021 crore. Notably, the bank's revenue grew at a 13% CAGR over the past five years, while net profit rose at a much faster CAGR of 72%. Alongside this, asset quality strengthened to a multi-year low, with Gross and Net NPA levels of 1.89% and 0.45%, respectively. The bank is also committed to sharing its financial success with shareholders. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now The bank maintains a clear policy to deliver periodic cash returns to its shareholders. For FY26, the Board recommended a dividend of ₹8.50 per share. In total, the bank paid a dividend of ₹4,395.7 crore during the year. It also boasts a Return on Equity of 15.39% and a Return on Assets consistently above 1%. Effectively, this public sector bank continues to balance capital appreciation with shareholder distributions. The bank is Bank of Baroda. Bank of Baroda Share Price Bank of Baroda Dividend Track Record: Why Profit Growth Outpaced Payouts Bank of Baroda paid a per-share dividend of ₹8.50 in FY26, translating into a dividend yield of 3.7% at the current price of ₹231.0. The bank issues a final dividend in June every year. Historically, the bank's per-share payout has almost surged 3x, from ₹2.85 in FY22 to ₹8.50 in FY26. In comparison, net profit grew by 2.75x during the period. Financial YearDividend/ShareNet ProfitPayout RatioFY22₹2.85₹7,272.0 crore19.0%FY23₹5.50₹14,110.0 crore19.0%FY24₹7.60₹17,784.0 crore22.1%FY25₹8.35₹19,581.0 crore22.0%FY26₹8.50₹20,021.0 crore22.0%Source: Annual Report The bank resumed dividend payments in FY22 after a four-year hiatus, following a period marked by high NPAs, elevated credit costs and losses. These challenges were common across the public sector banking space. The bank has also increased its payout ratio over the past five years, although at a slightly slower pace than its profitability. Core Operations: NII Inches Up 2.5% as Margin Contracts 19 bps to 2.89% Sustained financial growth enables Bank of Baroda to pay dividends. The bank's total business surged 13.9% year-on-year to ₹30,78,366 crore as global deposits grew 12.0% and advances surged 16.2%. Higher advances than deposits pushed the full-year Credit-Deposit ratio to a high of 91.65% against 88.56% in FY25 and 86.34% in FY24. The domestic Current Account Savings Account (CASA) ratio stood at 38.9%. Driven by strong business growth, the bank's total interest income grew 3.8% year-on-year to ₹126,994 crore. Of this, net interest income expanded 2.5% to ₹47,682 crore in FY26. Net Interest Margin (NIM), however, shrank by 19 bps to 2.89%. Source: Q4FY26 Investor Presentation The bank’s Cost-to-Income ratio also surged 121 bps to 49.15%, showing higher expenses. As a result, net profit grew only 2.2% to ₹20,021 crore. The Reserve Bank of India guidelines require dividends to be paid out of current-year net profits. In addition to net profits, dividend payouts depend directly on asset quality, capital adequacy metrics and regulatory guidelines. ALSO READAfter a decade without dividends, this PSU bank is back with a 3.8% yield Asset Quality Guardrails: Low NPAs Anchor Sustainable Cash Flows As of FY26, Retail, Agriculture, and MSME (RAM) financing accounts for 61.0% of gross domestic credit of ₹10,21,112 crore, while Corporate loans make up the remaining 39.0%. This mix has improved from FY25, when RAM advances held a 59.8% share. Balance Sheet Health: Why PCR at 93.9% Insulates Future Earnings About 96% of domestic advances above ₹50 crore carry external ratings of 'A and above’, which reduces default risk and stabilises asset performance. The bank's gross non-performing assets (NPAs) stood at a multi-year low of 1.89% (down from 2.26% as of Q4FY25), with net NPAs improving to 0.45% (down from 0.58%) in FY26. The bank’s Net NPA is well below the regulatory mandate of less than 7% required for dividend payout. The slippage ratio also fell by 6 bps to 0.72%, implying improved asset quality and fewer additions to stressed loans. A high provision coverage ratio (PCR) of 93.94% and ₹2,500 crore in floating provisions built up provide a strong buffer against any asset impairment losses. Overall, credit cost fell 1 bps to 0.46%. Keeping credit default risk low while maintaining strong capital buffers is key to sustaining asset quality, profitability and the bank’s capacity to distribute dividends. Deposit Profile: How a 38.9% CASA Base Shields Funding Costs At the same time, domestic deposits grew 12.8% year-on-year to ₹14,01,290 crore in FY26 (up from ₹12,42,169 crore in FY25), with domestic CASA at 38.9. This low-cost deposit base lowers the bank's funding costs, protects margins and also drives dividend payout. Capital Adequacy: 15.8% CRAR Provides Safe Headroom Over Basel III Norms Bank of Baroda's balance sheet maintains capital cushions comfortably above regulatory requirements, allowing consistent capital distribution to shareholders without restricting loan book expansion. In FY26, the Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) stood at 15.82%. CRAR further strengthened to 16.30% in Q1 FY27. The CRAR is significantly above the RBI-mandated threshold of 11.50% (including the mandatory 2.5% Capital Conservation Buffer). This robust capital cushion is one of the key factors the bank evaluates before declaring annual dividends. A

docs.title: SEBI gets 20,000 comments on CAS, market timings and derivatives settlement changes
docs.text: Markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on Saturday (October 3) said that it received as many as 20,000 comments on its consultation paper seeking public views on proposed changes to the Closing Auction Session (CAS), market timings and the settlement methodology for derivative contracts. The number of responses surged by the end of the consultation period, highlighting strong interest among market participants in the proposed changes. Taking to X, SEBI said, "The number of comments received till 7:00 PM today, i.e. October 3, 2026, stands at 20,000." The regulator had invited public comments on the proposals until October 3. Certain sections of media has reported regarding number of comments received on the Consultation paper on “Review of certain aspects of the Closing Auction Session, Market Timings and Settlement Methodologies for Derivative Contracts” as 3500, which was a few days back. The…— SecuritiesandExchangeBoardofIndia (@SEBI_updates) October 3, 2026 SEBI expects to move quickly on CAS framework The number of responses reached 20,000 by the end of the consultation period, higher than the over 3,500 comments that SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey had earlier said the regulator had received. Speaking at an event organised by the Commodity & Capital Market Participants Association of India (CPAI), Pandey said SEBI would examine the responses quickly and proceed with the next steps. "Today is the last date, and we will actually quickly look at all these comments and go ahead, because I think our proposals are quite clear," news agency PTI quoted Pandey as saying. Asked when the regulator could issue a final framework or circular on the CAS mechanism, Pandey indicated that it could happen soon. "Yes, it will be," he said when asked whether a circular could be expected shortly. ALSO READInvestors aware of market cycles: SEBI chief What is SEBI proposing on Closing Auction Session? In September, SEBI had proposed changes to the CAS framework as well as the methodology used to determine settlement prices for index and stock derivatives on expiry days. The review followed the introduction of the CAS in the equity cash segment and concerns raised over its potential impact on the settlement prices of derivative contracts. The Closing Auction Session is designed to determine the closing price of securities through an auction-based process. SEBI has said the proposed review is aimed at addressing specific issues emerging from the existing framework. The consultation paper also sought views from market participants on different possible approaches to resolving these concerns. Pandey reportedly said the consultation process was structured to address a clearly identified problem while giving stakeholders an opportunity to suggest alternative solutions. ALSO READSebi to review non-agri limits for liquidity boost SEBI pushes for deeper corporate bond derivatives market Separately, Pandey spoke about the development of the corporate bond derivatives market and said regulatory support, technological infrastructure and greater participation would be critical for the segment's growth. He said SEBI was working towards encouraging exchange-traded systems in the bond market. The regulator has already introduced several measures, including an electronic bidding platform for primary bond issuances, regulation of online bond platform providers and strengthening of the request-for-quote mechanism for secondary-market transactions. "Bond indices and derivatives and bond indices will be, I would think, at a major milestone going forward," Pandey said. ALSO READ2 Indian stocks up 205-690% as America builds more data centres and pipelines SEBI working with RBI to ease FPI access On Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) flows into India, Pandey said SEBI's role was to make it easier for overseas investors to enter and access the Indian market. However, he noted that investment decisions ultimately depend on the returns and opportunities available across different countries. Pandey said SEBI was working with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on measures aimed at further easing access for FPIs. The regulator has already taken several steps in this direction, including allowing FPIs to participate in non-agricultural commodity derivatives. Pandey said FPI holdings in India could rise or fall depending on investment opportunities across global markets. "All what we can do at the regulatory stage is to listen to what the FPIs have to say, easing their onboarding, easier the access," he said.

 The macroeconomic landscape has shifted considerably since the RBI’s August Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting. Both globally and domestically, growth has demonstrated commendable resilience — but that is only half the story. Persistent geopolitical tensions have tilted inflationary risks sharply to the upside, prompting central banks worldwide to recalibrate their actions and guidance. Across developed and emerging markets alike, bond yields are rising, even as policymakers and market participants debate the underlying drivers of this dislocation and how long financial systems can absorb the pressure from elevated rates.
Against this altered backdrop, we expect the RBI MPC to reverse the rate cycle at its October meeting. The question of whether rates will rise has largely been settled — the more nuanced debate now centres on the quantum of the hike, the stance, revised forecasts and forward guidance, liquidity management measures, and any signals around the RBI’s currency view. Before examining these finer points, it is worth recapping the case for a rate hike in October.
Even at the August MPC meeting, the RBI’s own projections pointed to headline inflation in the 5.5-6.0% range over the following three quarters. With policy rates left unchanged, this implies uncomfortably low real rates and risks the perception of the central bank falling behind the curve — particularly given the direction of travel among global central banks and the trajectory of sovereign yields. Meanwhile, with GDP growth printing at a robust 7.8% year-on-year in Q1FY27, the RBI has little reason to fear a significant growth sacrifice from a moderate tightening move. If the central bank was holding out for greater confidence in its inflation outlook, developments over the past two months have provided clarity — though not of the reassuring kind. Every material data point signals upside, not downside, risk to the consumer price index (CPI) trajectory.
It is now highly likely that the October MPC will see meaningful upward revisions to both FY27 growth and inflation forecasts. On growth, we see 30-50 basis points (bps) of upside risk to the RBI’s FY27 real GDP forecast of 6.7%, given that Q1FY27 alone came in 80 bps above the central bank’s own estimate of 7.0%. On inflation, September CPI is tracking around 5.6% year-on-year, implying Q2FY27 inflation at approximately 5.0% — already 30 bps ahead of the RBI’s forecast. But the risks extend well beyond the September print. 
The diffusion index in August CPI climbed to its highest level since the series began in 2015, raising the spectre of generalised inflation likely to weigh on the MPC’s deliberations. Global crude oil prices remain near $100 per barrel, and petrochemical product prices have rebounded to March-April levels, with consequences for input costs and consumer prices alike. Wholesale price index manufacturing inflation, running above 8%, could eventually filter through to still-subdued CPI core goods inflation. 
A deficient monsoon is pressuring kharif crop prices, and with a strong El Niño expected to persist into early next year, risks to the winter crop are equally concerning. The World Bank’s EM Food Price Index has swung from -0.3% year-on-year in February to 11.5% in August — a reversal that cannot be ignored. Taken together, we see approximately 20 bps of upside risk to the RBI’s core inflation forecast of 4.3% for FY27, and around 10 bps to the headline forecast of 5.0%. The semi-annual Monetary Policy Report, due alongside the October decision, will provide the RBI’s first quarterly inflation estimates for FY28 — a critical input for markets gauging ex-ante real rates and the policy path into 2027 — and may also include a reassessment of the neutral rate.
The current MPC has consistently used the policy stance as a forward guidance tool, signalling the direction and duration of the rate cycle rather than committing to a terminal rate. October may be premature for the committee to declare a definitive endpoint. A neutral stance preserves flexibility and allows the MPC to frame a potential hike as a recalibration rather than the opening salvo of a prolonged tightening cycle. December, with the benefit of additional data, would be a more appropriate moment for a stance reassessment. Even so, the parameters the RBI flags as conditions for future hikes will be closely watched.
On liquidity, our projections suggest the current exceptional durable surplus will organically moderate by Q4FY27. It would therefore be prudent to allow overnight rates to adjust gradually toward the repo rate, rather than forcing an immediate convergence through aggressive withdrawal. Short-tenor sell/buy FX swaps and other FX interventions are likely to remain the primary absorption tools, offering maximum flexibility — though their effectiveness will be tempered by the limited depth of these markets. Additional open market operations sales of approximately `1.0 trillion are also possible, with an announcement potentially accompanying the policy statement.
If the MPC opts for a front-loaded 50-bps hike — premised on a baseline of 100 bps of cumulative tightening — it would carry hawkish overtones for markets, and would likely need to be accompanied by a stance shift to “calibrated tightening” and more assertive liquidity absorption. While such a package could bolster the RBI’s inflation-fighting credibility and support the currency in an era of rising global yields, it may be too aggressive a step so early in the cycle. Historically, the RBI tightening phases tend to be shallower and less protracted than those of its global counterparts, often reversing previous rate cuts without doing so in their entirety.

docs.title: Tejas Mk-1A delays will ‘hurt us’: IAF chief flags impact as fighter squadrons fall to 29
docs.text: India has already committed well over Rs 1.1 lakh crore to two big Tejas Mk‑1A deals that were supposed to start delivering fighter jets years ago, but not a single aircraft has reached the Indian Air Force (IAF) so far. Against this backdrop of stalled spending and shrinking squadron strength, IAF chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh on Saturday (October 3) said the delays in the Tejas programme have been significant and are now directly affecting the force’s combat readiness. Speaking at the annual press conference ahead of the 94th Air Force Day, AP Singh made it clear that while some slippage is normal in defence projects, the current situation is unusually severe. “It happens that you plan something, but things get delayed. But this time, the delay has been much,” he said, adding, “We are also looking towards Mark 2. All these will be able to fill in the gaps that exist.” #WATCH | On whether HAL will be penalised for the delays in LCA Mark 1A, IAF chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh says, "It happens that you plan something, but things get delayed. But this time, the delay has been much. We are also looking towards Mark 2. All these will be able to fill in the gaps that exist."— ANI (@ANI) October 3, 2026 Big money, zero jets: The Tejas Mk‑1A contracts at a glance The financial scale of the delay is stark: In February 2021, the defence ministry signed a Rs 48,000 crore contract with Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd (HAL) for 83 Tejas Mk‑1A jets (73 fighters and 10 trainers). Deliveries were to begin by 2024. In September 2025, a second deal worth Rs 62,370 crore was signed for 97 more Mk‑1A aircraft, further expanding the order book. Together, these contracts tie up more than Rs 1.1 lakh crore of defence spending on a platform that has yet to enter IAF service in its Mk‑1A form. As of early October 2026, no Mk‑1A jet has been formally handed over to the IAF, even though the first deliveries were due over two years ago. ALSO READRs 235 cr missile bet, Rs 4.3 cr robot bet: Singhania and Kedia’s new picks revealed The defence ministry has already warned that HAL could face liquidated damages (contractual penalties) for missing delivery schedules, after imposing similar penalties on engine supplier GE for its own delays. 'It is going to hurt us': IAF chief on squadron shortfall The human and operational cost of these delays is visible in the IAF’s depleting fighter strength. Singh said the force now has only 29 fighter squadrons, far below the 42 squadrons officially sanctioned to handle a two‑front threat from China and Pakistan. To simply stop the decline and begin rebuilding, the IAF needs to induct 36–40 new fighter jets every year for the next few years, he said. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year. That means anything between 36 and 40 aircraft should be produced and inducted into the IAF for us to stop going down from the current 30 fighter squadrons and start improving towards the target of 42 squadrons. Actually, we need even more than that,” Singh said. On the Tejas Mk‑1A specifically, he added, “There is some extra delay, and there is no doubt that it is going to hurt us.” ALSO READBeyond airlines: 2 high-ROCE SMEs riding India’s private jet and pilot training boom Beyond Mk‑1A: Mk‑2, AMCA, MRFA and even Su‑57 on the table With Mk‑1A deliveries lagging, the IAF is pinning its hopes on multiple parallel programmes: Tejas Mk‑2: A more powerful, medium-weight fighter still under development. Singh confirmed the force is “also looking towards Mark 2” to help close capability gaps. AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft): India’s indigenous fifth‑generation stealth fighter programme. MRFA (Multi‑Role Fighter Aircraft): The plan to buy 114 foreign fighters, now centred on the Rafale under a government‑to‑government deal with France. Singh said he hopes the MRFA deal can be signed within this financial year if negotiations go smoothly. “I think if things go well, we should be able to sign MRFA deal in this financial year. That’s what my hope is. But it is a two-way process,” he said, referring to talks between India and France. At the same time, he also flagged a contingency plan if AMCA faces delays. “If there are delays in the AMCA fifth-generation fighter programme, we may have to look at other options. Russia has offered the Su‑57, but no decision has been taken yet,” he said. #WATCH | Indian Air Force chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh holds annual press conference in Delhi, says, "If there are delays in the AMCA fifth-generation fighter programme, we may have to look at other options. Russia has offered the Su-57, but no decision has been taken yet. We… pic.twitter.com/ehOO652f6A— ANI (@ANI) October 3, 2026 Neighbour’s stealth jets: 'A cause for worry' IAF Chief Singh also expressed concern over regional developments, particularly reports of Pakistan collaborating with China on advanced and fifth‑generation fighter projects, while China already operates stealth jets like the J‑20 and is developing others. “It is a cause for worry,” he said, while adding, “We do have capabilities. It is not that one platform matters so much.” Now, India needs to speed up both home-grown and foreign fighter programmes to maintain its defence capability. We have been working towards it, and we have been a part of discussions throughout,” he said. docs.title: IDBI Bank, Lal PathLabs, Welspun Living: Top stock ideas by Choice Broking
docs.text:
IDBI Bank, Lal PathLabs, Welspun Living: Top stock ideas by Choice Broking
 Stocks to buy today: IDBI Bank has moved above both its 50-day EMA, which indicates that the near-term trend is turning positive, says Sachin Gupta of Choice Broking.
 Stocks to buy today: Choice Broking is bullish on IDBI Bank, Dr Lal PathLabs and Welspun Living.
 Sachin Gupta Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 05 2026 | 7:35 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Disclaimer: This article is written by Sachin Gupta, VP – technical research at Choice Broking. Views expressed are his own. Readers' discretion is advised. Stocks to buy today - Recommendations by Sachin Gupta, Choice Broking IDBI Bank
Buy IDBI in cash around ₹87 | SL ₹81 | TGT ₹92/95 IDBI Bank is showing a noticeable improvement in its technical setup on the daily chart, with the stock gaining over 5 per cent in the latest session and attracting strong buying interest. The stock has moved above both its 50-day EMA, which indicates that the near-term trend is turning positive. The price is also holding above the rising trendline that has been supporting the stock during recent dips. Momentum has improved as well, with RSI at 55.87, while the rise in trading volume adds further strength to the current move. Hence, trader can consider buying around ₹87 with a stop-loss at ₹₹81. The ₹81–82 zone is likely to act as an important support area. On the upside, the stock could gradually move towards ₹92–95 levels. Dr. Lal Path Labs
Buy LALPATHLAB in cash at ₹2,005 | SL ₹1,900 | TGT ₹2,100/2150 Dr. Lal Patha Labs is looking positive on the daily chart, with the stock holding close to its recent high and trading comfortably above both the 50-day EMA of ₹1,882.90 and the 200-day EMA of ₹1,679. The recent price action shows that buying interest remains intact, while the RSI at 67.22 also supports the positive momentum. The stock has maintained its upward trend and is showing strength even at higher levels. At the current market price of around ₹2,005, the stock can be considered for buying with a stop-loss at ₹1,900. The ₹1,930–₹1,950 zone should act as an important support area. On the upside, the stock can move towards ₹2,100–₹2,150 levels. Welspun Living
Buy WELSPUNLIV in cash at ₹233-231 | SL ₹223 | TGT ₹250 Welspun Living is maintaining a strong bullish structure on the daily chart, with the stock continuing to form higher tops and higher bottoms while trading near its all-time highs. In Thursday's session, the stock broke above its recent swing highs on strong volumes and gained more than 5 per cent, indicating renewed buying interest and strength in the ongoing uptrend. However, the RSI is currently at an elevated level, so some profit booking or a period of sideways consolidation cannot be ruled out in the near term. Despite this, the overall price structure remains positive, and any meaningful dip could provide a buying opportunity. Traders can consider buying the stock around ₹233– 231, with a stop-loss at ₹223 and an upside target of ₹250.

docs.title: Top 3 stocks to buy: HDFC Bank, Infosys, BEL by Ganesh Dongre | Target price, stop-loss for IT, defence and bank shares
docs.text:
Ganesh Dongre, Assistant Vice President — Equity Research at Anand Rathi, believes the Nifty has moved into an oversold zone following the recent sharp decline. The correction has been driven by a combination of global risk-off sentiment and concerns surrounding the US Federal Reserve’s interest-rate outlook. The possibility of further rate hikes in the coming quarters remains a key concern for global equity markets, while the upward bias in the US 10-year Treasury yield could continue to influence risk appetite and foreign fund flows. On the outlook of the Nifty 50 index, Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said, the Nifty 50 index continues to face strong resistance in the 23,500–23,600 zone, which also coincides with the broader 200-day EMA resistance area. The index recently slipped towards 22,500, close to the previous low set in March 2026, suggesting the market is approaching an important technical support level. A sustained weekly close above 23,000 would help improve the near-term technical setup and could open the possibility of a recovery towards the 23,800–24,200 zone. “On the downside, 22,000–22,200 remains an important support zone, as this region represents a previous significant support area. Given the sharp correction and oversold conditions, the market could witness bouts of volatility followed by sideways consolidation in the coming weeks,” said Dongre. On the outlook for the Bank Nifty today, Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said, the key benchmark index remained under significant selling pressure and continues to trade below its 200-day EMA around 56,400, making this an important technical zone to monitor. The index is currently positioned near a crucial support area, with the next major support placed around 52,700. On the upside, 56,000–56,500 remains an important resistance zone. “A decisive and sustained breakout above 56,500 would strengthen the near-term technical structure and could indicate the possibility of a recovery towards higher levels. Until such a breakout occurs, volatility and selling pressure at higher levels cannot be ruled out,” the Anand Rathi expert said. Regarding stocks to buy on Monday, Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi recommended these three top stocks: HDFC Bank , Infosys , and BEL . 1] HDFC Bank: Buy at ₹ 710 to ₹ 720 | Target ₹ 760 | Stop Loss ₹ 680; 2] Infosys: Buy at ₹ 1020 to ₹ 1040 | Target ₹ 1180 | Stop Loss ₹ 980; and 3] BEL: Buy at ₹ 390 to ₹ 395 | Target ₹ 410 | Stop Loss ₹ 380. Disclaimer: This story is for educational and informational purposes only. The views and recommendations above are those of individual analysts or broking companies, not Mint. We advise investors to check with certified financial experts before making any investment decisions. Asit Manohar has nearly two decades of experience in the mainstream media. In this period, he has served esteemed media organisations like NDTV Profit, The Economic Times, and Zee Business. He has been working at LiveMint Digital since April 2021. During these two decades of journey in mainstream media, Asit has mainly covered external affairs, markets and personal finance. However, his earliest beats include railways, SME, MSME, and politics (Congress beat). Some of his features on political, economic, and foreign policy are documented in the parliamentary records.

While pursuing his MA (Mass Communication, Session 2004-06), Asit began his media career as a stringer at All India Radio in Varanasi. At AIR Varanasi, Asit worked with the Gyanvani, Yuvvani and Vividh Bharti teams. After working for nearly one year at AIR Varanasi, he shifted to print journalism and started working as a stringer for the HT Media Ltd, Varanasi. At HT Media Ltd in Varanasi, he covered the BHU beat.

Asit has also worked with some brokerage houses. He has worked with Religare Broking and India Infoline, where he assisted the research team in developing and executing trade strategies for intraday cash, F&O, and commodities.

Asit is a Gold Medalist in MA (Mass Communication) from BHU, Varanasi. He did his BSc. (Hons) in Mathematics from Magadh University, Bodh Gaya.
